<!-- mainthm-1: body_md -->
Both $\Sigma_+(7)$ and $\Sigma_-(7)$ are diffeomorphic to $S^4$. Their belt
spheres $K_+,K_-\subset S^4$ are smooth fibred two-knots with fundamental
quandle $P_7$, knot group $G_7$, and fibre $N_7\setminus\operatorname{int} D^3$. Their unpointed closed monodromy class
(Definition~\ref{def:fibred}) is represented by the order-six isometry
$\bar f$.

Although the two knots have diffeomorphic exteriors, they are not equivalent
(Definition~\ref{def:equivalence}) for any choice of orientations. Thus neither
knot is determined by its exterior. In fact, no homeomorphism of pairs
identifies them (Remark~\ref{eval:rem:topological}). This topological assertion uses
the homotopy invariance of Teichner's secondary invariant
\cite[Theorem~6.4.1]{Teichner1992}. Every smooth oriented fibred
two-knot with quandle $P_7$ in a smooth homotopy four-sphere is equivalent to exactly one of them, possibly after
reversing the knot orientation.
<!-- end mainthm-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:weight}
An element of a group is a \emph{weight element} if its normal closure is
the whole group; its orbit under the automorphism group is a
\emph{weight orbit}. If $G^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong\mathbb Z$ and an epimorphism
$\epsilon:G\to\mathbb Z$ has been fixed, a \emph{positive strict weight orbit}
is an orbit of
$
 \operatorname{Aut}_\epsilon(G)=\{\eta\in\operatorname{Aut}(G):\epsilon\circ\eta=\epsilon\}
$
on the weight elements $w$ with $\epsilon(w)=1$.
An automorphism $\varphi$ of a group $H$ is \emph{meridianal} if
$
 \langle\!\langle h^{-1}\varphi(h)\mid h\in H\rangle\!\rangle=H.
$
Equivalently, the subgroup generated by these elements is $H$, since
that subgroup is normal in $H$.
These are the conventions of
\cite[Sections~14.7--14.8]{Hillman} and
\cite[Definition~12.41, Definition~14.1 and Lemma~14.2(i)]{QextC}.
For $G_7$, the epimorphism $\epsilon$ is the degree homomorphism sending
$t$ to $1$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:equivalence}
Smooth oriented two-knots $K\subset\Sigma$ and $K'\subset\Sigma'$ in smooth
homotopy four-spheres are \emph{equivalent}, or \emph{diffeomorphic as pairs},
if some diffeomorphism $\Sigma\to\Sigma'$ carries $K$ onto $K'$, preserving the
orientations of the knots; no condition is imposed on the orientations of
$\Sigma$ and $\Sigma'$. The qualification ``possibly after reversing the knot
orientation'' drops the condition on the knot orientations as well.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:fibred}
Let $K$ be a smooth two-knot in a smooth homotopy four-sphere $\Sigma$, let
$X=\Sigma\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu K$ be its exterior, and identify $\partial X$ with
$K\times S^1$ so that each circle $\{x\}\times S^1$ is a meridian.

Such a trivialization exists in the present setting. Indeed,
$H_2(\Sigma;\mathbb Z)=0$, so the self-intersection number of $K$ is zero. Hence the
Euler class of the oriented normal $2$-plane bundle of $K$ vanishes; since
oriented real $2$-plane bundles over $S^2$ are classified by their Euler class,
the normal bundle is trivial.
This identification is induced by a trivialization
$\nu K\cong K\times D^2$ and is unique up to isotopy once the orientation
of the meridians is fixed, because tubular neighbourhoods are unique up to
isotopy \cite[Chapter~4, Section~5]{Hirsch} and $[S^2,SO(2)]=0$. The knot
is \emph{fibred} if $X$ admits a smooth fibre bundle projection
$p_X\colon X\to S^1$ whose restriction to $\partial X$ is the projection
$K\times S^1\to S^1$. A meridian maps with degree one, so
$(p_X)_*:\pi_1(X)\to\pi_1(S^1)$ is surjective. The homotopy exact
sequence of the bundle then implies that its fibre $F$ is connected.
Thus $F$ is a compact connected three-manifold with
$\partial F\cong S^2$; the \emph{closed fibre} is
$\widehat F=F\cup_{\partial}D^3$.
A \emph{return map} is the first-return map $h\colon F\to F$ of the flow
of a vector field on $X$ that projects to the unit vector field of $S^1$
and agrees with its product lift on a fixed boundary collar. The map $h$
fixes a collar of $\partial F$ pointwise, and $X$ is the
mapping torus of $h$. For a fixed bundle projection $p_X$, a fixed
reference fibre and a fixed product collar, the allowed vector fields
form a convex set. A path between two such fields gives an isotopy
between their return maps, fixed on that collar. Changing the
identification of the reference fibre conjugates the return map.
This uniqueness statement is relative to the chosen fibration. Extending
$h$ by the identity of $D^3$ gives the \emph{closed monodromy}
$\hat h\colon\widehat F\to\widehat F$. Its isotopy class in
$\operatorname{Diff}(\widehat F)$, where isotopies need not fix $D^3$ or any point, taken
up to conjugation by diffeomorphisms of $\widehat F$, is the
\emph{unpointed closed monodromy class} of the fibration.
The class is also independent of the choice of product collar. If $c_0$ and
$c_1$ are two product collars of $\partial X$ compatible with $p_X$, then
$(c_0)_*\partial_t$ and $(c_1)_*\partial_t$ are inward-pointing vector
fields tangent to the fibres of $p_X$. Interpolating linearly between them
and integrating, as in the proof that collars are unique up to isotopy
(compare \cite[Chapter~4, Section~6]{Hirsch}), gives a diffeomorphism $\Psi$
of $X$ that maps each fibre of $p_X$ to itself, is the identity on
$\partial X$ and satisfies $\Psi\circ c_0=c_1$ near $\partial X$. Then
$\Psi_*$ carries the allowed vector fields for $c_0$ to those for $c_1$, the
corresponding return maps are conjugate by $\Psi|_F$, and
$\Psi|_F\cup\mathrm{id}_{D^3}$ is a diffeomorphism between the closed fibres formed
with the collars $c_0$ and $c_1$ that conjugates the closed monodromies.
Both $\widehat F$ and its unpointed closed monodromy class are
independent of the gluing $\partial F\cong\partial D^3$: every diffeomorphism of $S^2$ extends over
$D^3$ \cite{Smale1959}, and if $\Phi$ extends the change of gluing, then
$\mathrm{id}_F\cup\Phi$ identifies the two closed fibres and conjugates one closed
monodromy to the other, both being the identity on $D^3$.
A \emph{geometric monodromy} is any diffeomorphism $c$ of $F$, not
necessarily fixing $\partial F$ pointwise, such that $X$ is diffeomorphic
over $S^1$ to the mapping torus of $c$; it has \emph{finite order} if $c$
is periodic.

The notation $c$, $c_0$, $c_1$, $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ has the meanings given above
only within this definition. Elsewhere in
Sections~\ref{sec:construction} and~\ref{sec:rigidity}, $c$ is the
generator of $C_7$, $c_0$ is the projected geodesic of
Section~\ref{sec:construction}, and $\Phi$ is the involution of
Lemma~\ref{lem:weight-loops}.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:group-data}
The element $t$ normally generates $G_7$, and
$G_7^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong\mathbb Z$, generated by the class of $t$.
Consequently $G_7'=\Gamma$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
This is the parameter-seven specialization of
\cite[Proposition~14.22 and Theorem~14.24, pp.~241--244]{QextC}; in the
convention \eqref{eq:group}, the meridianal automorphism is $\theta$ and the
stable letter $t$ is the positive weight element.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
For $g=(q,c^a)\in\Gamma$, the convention \eqref{eq:group} gives
\[
 [g,t]=g^{-1}t^{-1}gt=g^{-1}\theta(g)=\bigl(q^{-1}\alpha(q),\,c^{-2a}\bigr).
\]
For $g=(i,1)$, $(j,1)$ and $(1,c)$ this yields $(-k,1)$, $(-i,1)$ and
$(1,c^{-2})$. The first two generate $Q_8$, and $c^{-2}$ generates $C_7$
because $2$ is invertible modulo $7$. Hence these commutators generate
$\Gamma$, and $\theta$ is meridianal in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:weight}. Since each $[g,t]$ belongs to $\langle\!\langle t\rangle\!\rangle$, we obtain
$\Gamma\subseteq\langle\!\langle t\rangle\!\rangle$ and therefore $\langle\!\langle t\rangle\!\rangle=G_7$. Likewise
$\Gamma\subseteq G_7'$, while $G_7/\Gamma\cong\mathbb Z$ is abelian. Hence
$G_7'=\Gamma$, and $G_7^{\mathrm{ab}}=G_7/\Gamma\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by
the class of $t$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:frame}
The framing \eqref{eq:frame} closes smoothly across the mapping-torus
seam. Replacing $u(s)$ by
$u_-(s)=\exp(3\pi j\,r(s)/2)$ gives the other homotopy class of
framings, denoted by $\lambda_-$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
At the endpoints, $V_a(0)=f(1)a$ and $V_a(1)=jaj^{-1}$.
Since $df_1(w)=\omega^{-1}wj$, we have
\[
                  df_1(V_a(1))=\omega^{-1}ja=f(1)a=V_a(0).
\]
Since $\widetilde c$ and $r$ are constant near $0$ and $1$, the frames
match smoothly across a collar of the seam.
The frame defined by $u_-$ closes in the same way: $u_-(0)=1$ and
$u_-(1)=\exp(3\pi j/2)=-j$, so its vectors at $s=0$ and $s=1$ are again
$f(1)a$ and $(-j)a(-j)^{-1}=jaj^{-1}$, and the displayed identity applies
verbatim. Equivalently, the loop $A$ below satisfies $A(0)=A(1)=\mathrm{id}$.
The two frames differ by the loop
\[
 A(s)(a)=\exp(\pi j\,r(s))\,a\,\exp(-\pi j\,r(s))
                      \;\;\text{in }SO(3).
\]
Under the double covering $S^3\to SO(3)$ given by quaternionic
conjugation, the lift of $A$ starting at $1$ is
$s\mapsto\exp(\pi j\,r(s))$ and ends at $-1$.
Thus $A$ is not null-homotopic and represents the nonzero class of
$\pi_1(SO(3))\cong\mathbb Z/2$; equivalently, use
$SO(3)\cong\mathbb{RP}^3$ and
\cite[Example~1.43]{Hatcher}.
Once a reference framing has been fixed, any other oriented framing is represented
by a map $S^1\to SO(3)$. Hence the set of homotopy classes is
$[S^1,SO(3)]\cong\pi_1(SO(3))\cong\mathbb Z/2$, so these are exactly the two
normal-framing classes.
These two classes are taken among the framings that induce on the normal
bundle of $\gamma$ the orientation determined by $\lambda_+$. Framings
inducing the opposite orientation are treated at the end of the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:weight-loops}, where they are shown to give the same
surgery pairs up to the orientation of the belt sphere.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:exists}
Both $\Sigma_+(7)$ and $\Sigma_-(7)$ are smooth homotopy four-spheres. Their belt
spheres have the common fibred exterior $E_7$, with fibre
$N_7\setminus\operatorname{int} D^3$, and
\[
                  Q(\Sigma_\varepsilon(7),K_\varepsilon)\cong P_7.
\]
Moreover $\operatorname{As}(P_7)\cong G_7$. In particular both ambient manifolds are
homeomorphic to $S^4$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The preceding surgery calculation proves that both ambient manifolds
are smooth homotopy four-spheres. The fibrewise neighbourhood and the
attaching maps give the common fibred exterior $E_7$, with fibre
$N_7\setminus\operatorname{int} D^3$. Its peripheral subgroup is $\langle t\rangle$,
since the boundary circle is the positive meridian and
$\pi_1(S^2\times S^1)\cong\mathbb Z$. The peripheral coset description
\eqref{eq:coset} therefore identifies its fundamental quandle with $P_7$.
These are also the parameter-seven conclusions of
\cite[Definition~18.3 and Proposition~18.4(i), pp.~358--359]{QextC}.
Under the knot-quandle dictionary
\cite[Section~3, (3.3), pp.~45--47]{QextC}, the associated-group
isomorphism is the marked isomorphism
\[
 \operatorname{As}(P_7)\to G_7,\;\;\; e_x\longmapsto x^{-1}tx
 \;\;(x\in\Gamma).
\]
In particular $e_1$ maps to the positive meridian $t$, and the canonical
augmentation sending each $e_x$ to $1$ agrees with the degree
homomorphism of $G_7$.
Freedman's theorem identifies both ambient manifolds topologically with
$S^4$ \cite{Freedman}.
Lemma~\ref{lem:As-twoknot} and Remark~\ref{rem:As-algebraic} at the end of
this section give a proof of $\operatorname{As}(P_7)\cong G_7$ that uses neither the
knot--quandle dictionary nor the coset enumeration of
Remark~\ref{rem:As-direct}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:As-direct}
The isomorphism $\operatorname{As}(P_7)\cong G_7$ can also be verified without the
knot-quandle dictionary. By \eqref{eq:group}, $xy^{-1}ty=t\,\theta(xy^{-1})y$
for $x,y\in\Gamma$, so $x*y=t^{-1}w$ with $w=xy^{-1}ty$, and hence
$(x*y)^{-1}t\,(x*y)=w^{-1}tw=(y^{-1}ty)^{-1}(x^{-1}tx)(y^{-1}ty)$. Thus
$e_x\mapsto x^{-1}tx$ defines a homomorphism $\operatorname{As}(P_7)\to G_7$; it is
surjective because $\langle\!\langle t\rangle\!\rangle=G_7$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:group-data}). Its kernel
$\mathcal K$ meets $\langle e_1\rangle$ trivially, since $e_1\mapsto t$ has
infinite order; hence $[\operatorname{As}(P_7):\langle e_1\rangle]=56\,|\mathcal K|$. If
$S\subset P_7$ generates $P_7$ as a quandle, the relations
$e_{x*s}=e_s^{-1}e_xe_s$ with $x\in P_7$ and $s\in S$ imply all defining
relations of $\operatorname{As}(P_7)$: the identities $x*(a*b)=((x*^{-1}b)*a)*b$ and
$x*(a*^{-1}b)=((x*b)*a)*^{-1}b$ show that the set of $y$ for which
$e_{x*y}=e_y^{-1}e_xe_y$ holds for all $x$ is closed under $*$ and $*^{-1}$.
For $S=\{1,(i,c)\}$, which generates $P_7$, a Todd--Coxeter enumeration of
the cosets of $\langle e_1\rangle$ in the resulting presentation, with $56$
generators and $112$ relators, closes with $56$ cosets. Hence
$\mathcal K=1$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:closed-vs-punctured-monodromy}
The order-six map $\bar f$ is a representative of the unpointed closed
monodromy class \cite[Proposition~15.24, pp.~275--276]{QextC}.
Indeed, a ball-moving isotopy along the section identifies the moving
deleted ball with a fixed ball. In that trivialization the return map
extends over the ball to a diffeomorphism isotopic, as an unpointed map,
to $\bar f$; see \cite[Remark~18.15, p.~367]{QextC}. The ball-moving
isotopy may change the pointed representative, while preserving this
unpointed isotopy class. It should not
be confused with a finite-order monodromy of the punctured fibre. For the
prism family with parameter greater than one, such periodic exterior
monodromy is excluded by \cite[Proposition~15.21, pp.~273--274]{QextC}; the
relation between the closed representative and a boundary-fixing return map
is recorded in \cite[Remark~18.15, p.~367]{QextC}. Accordingly, every
occurrence of ``period six'' below refers to the closed monodromy class or to
its displayed representative $\bar f$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:monodromy-direct}
Both statements of Remark~\ref{rem:closed-vs-punctured-monodromy} can be
checked directly in the present coordinates.

\emph{The unpointed closed monodromy class of $p_{E_7}$ contains $\bar f$.}
Fix $\varepsilon$. Since the radius of $\nu\gamma$ may be chosen small,
we may assume that $T_\varepsilon$ extends, by the same formula, to an
embedding of $S^1\times 2D^3$ with $p(T_\varepsilon(s,z))=s$, where $rD^3$
denotes the closed ball of radius $r$. Let $Y_0$ be the vector field on $M_7$ induced by
$\partial_s$ on $S^3\times\mathbb R$. Since $(v,1)=D(f(v),0)$, the time-one flow
of $Y_0$ sends $[v,0]$ to $[f(v),0]$, so its first-return map on
$p^{-1}(0)=N_7$ is $\bar f$. The condition $dp(Y)=\partial_s$ is convex, so a
partition of unity gives a vector field $Y$ on $M_7$ with $dp(Y)=\partial_s$
that equals $dT_\varepsilon(\partial_s)$ on
$T_\varepsilon\bigl(S^1\times\tfrac32D^3\bigr)$. Its restriction to $E_7$ is
an allowed vector field in Definition~\ref{def:fibred}, for the fibration
$p_{E_7}$ and the product collar
$T_\varepsilon\bigl(S^1\times(\tfrac32D^3\setminus\operatorname{int} D^3)\bigr)$
determined by $\phi_\varepsilon$; let $h$ be its return map. In the ball
coordinates $z\mapsto T_\varepsilon(0,z)$, the first-return map of $Y$ on
$p^{-1}(0)$ is $h\cup\mathrm{id}_{D^3}$, which is a closed monodromy. The fields
$(1-\tau)Y_0+\tau Y$, $0\le\tau\le1$, all project to $\partial_s$, and their
first-return maps form an isotopy, not required to fix any point, from
$\bar f$ to $h\cup\mathrm{id}_{D^3}$.

\emph{There is no geometric monodromy of finite order.} Let
$\sigma\colon F\to F$ be a geometric monodromy of finite order for
$p_{E_7}$, so that $\widehat F=N_7$. The mapping torus of $\sigma$ is
diffeomorphic to the orientable manifold $E_7$, so $\sigma$ preserves
orientation. Averaging a metric over $\langle\sigma\rangle$ gives a
$\sigma$-invariant product collar of $\partial F\cong S^2$, and, by
uniformization, the restriction of $\sigma$ to $\partial F$ is smoothly
conjugate to a conformal map of finite order of the round sphere, hence to
an element of $SO(3)$. Coning over the collar therefore extends $\sigma$ to
a smooth periodic diffeomorphism $\hat\sigma$ of $\widehat F$ with a fixed
point, the cone point.

More explicitly, let $a=\sigma|_{\partial F}$. Choose a diffeomorphism
$\Xi\colon S^2\to S^2$ and a rotation $R\in SO(3)$ such that $\Xi a\Xi^{-1}=R$.
Using the $\sigma$-invariant collar and the extension consequence of
\cite{Smale1959}, extend $\Xi$ over the capping ball by a diffeomorphism
$H:D^3\to D^3$ that is product-like near its boundary. On the
cap use $H^{-1}RH$. Its boundary restriction is $a$, so it glues smoothly to
$\sigma$ across the product collar; moreover it has finite order, and it fixes
the point corresponding under $H$ to the centre of the linear rotation.
Thus the resulting extension $\hat\sigma$ is indeed a smooth periodic
diffeomorphism of $\widehat F$ with a fixed point. By \cite[Theorem~E and Section~2.1]{DinkelbachLeeb},
$\hat\sigma$ is smoothly conjugate to an orientation-preserving isometry
$\bar g$ of $N_7$, which then also has a fixed point.

Since $E_7$ is diffeomorphic over $S^1$ to the mapping torus of $\sigma$, the
outer automorphism of $\pi_1(F)=\pi_1(\widehat F)\cong\Gamma$ induced by
$\sigma$ is, up to an automorphism of $\Gamma$, the class of conjugation by
an element of degree $\pm1$ of $G_7$, that is, $[\theta]^{\pm1}$. Hence
$\bar g$ induces an $\operatorname{Aut}(\Gamma)$-conjugate of $[\theta]^{\pm1}$. As
$\operatorname{Out}(\Gamma)=\operatorname{Out}(Q_8)\times\operatorname{Aut}(C_7)$ and $[\theta]=([\alpha],-1)$, the
outer automorphism induced by $\bar g$ has the form $([\alpha'],-1)$, where
$[\alpha']\in\operatorname{Out}(Q_8)$ has order three.

Lift $\bar g$ to $g(v)=AvB$ with $A,B\in S^3$. The preimage of $\Gamma$ in
$S^3\times S^3$ is $Q_8\times\langle-\zeta\rangle$, which $g$ normalizes
factorwise. Moreover $g\gamma_{q,0}g^{-1}=\gamma_{AqA^{-1},0}$, and
$g\gamma_{1,1}g^{-1}$ is right multiplication by $B^{-1}\zeta^{-1}B$. The
normalizer of $Q_8$ in $S^3$ is the binary octahedral group; it maps onto
$\operatorname{Out}(Q_8)\cong S_3$ with kernel $Q_8$, and the elements mapping to elements
of order three are those of $\langle i,j,\omega\rangle\setminus Q_8$, the
sixteen quaternions $\tfrac12(\pm1\pm i\pm j\pm k)$. Since conjugation by
$A$ induces $[\alpha']$ on $Q_8$, we get $\operatorname{Re}(A)=\pm\tfrac12$. Since the
$C_7$-component of the induced automorphism is inversion,
$g\gamma_{1,1}g^{-1}=\gamma_{1,-1}$, that is, $B^{-1}\zeta B=\zeta^{-1}$;
thus conjugation by $B$ is a rotation sending $i$ to $-i$, so
$B\in\mathbb R j+\mathbb R k$ and $\operatorname{Re}(B)=0$. The other lifts $\gamma_{q,m}\circ g$ are
the maps $v\mapsto(qA)\,v\,(B\zeta^{-m})$, and $qA$ and $B\zeta^{-m}$ are
again of these two kinds. By Lemma~\ref{per:lem:rigidity}, no lift has a
fixed point. Hence $\bar g$ is fixed-point free, a contradiction.

The same argument applies to any fibration of $E_7$ as in
Definition~\ref{def:fibred}, since its closed fibre is again diffeomorphic
to $N_7$ by Remark~\ref{rem:rigidity-outline}(b).
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:As-twoknot}
Let $K$ be a smooth oriented two-knot in a smooth homotopy four-sphere
$\Sigma$, with exterior $X$, knot group $\pi=\pi_1(X)$, positive meridian
$m\in\pi$ and peripheral subgroup $P\le\pi$. Identify $Q(\Sigma,K)$ with the
peripheral coset quandle $P\backslash\pi$, $Pg*Ph=P\,gh^{-1}mh$
\cite{Joyce,WinterHigher}, as in \eqref{eq:coset}. Then $P=\langle m\rangle$, and
\[
 \kappa\colon\operatorname{As}(Q(\Sigma,K))\to\pi,\;\;\; e_{Pg}\longmapsto g^{-1}mg,
\]
is a well-defined isomorphism carrying each generator $e_x$ to a meridian.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
For oriented codimension-two knots in the standard sphere, the
isomorphism between the associated group of the fundamental quandle
and the knot group is classical; see
\cite[Theorem~4.1]{Kamada2014} and the earlier work
\cite{Joyce,FennRourke1992}; see also \cite{WinterHigher}.
We include the argument to make explicit the formulation needed here
for a two-knot in an arbitrary smooth homotopy four-sphere.

Write $Q=Q(\Sigma,K)$. The subgroup $P$ is the image of
$\pi_1(\partial X)\cong\pi_1(S^2\times S^1)\cong\mathbb Z$, which is generated by
the meridian, so $P=\langle m\rangle$ and $g^{-1}mg$ depends only on $Pg$.
Since
\[
 \kappa(e_{Pg*Ph})=(gh^{-1}mh)^{-1}\,m\,(gh^{-1}mh)
 =\kappa(e_{Ph})^{-1}\kappa(e_{Pg})\kappa(e_{Ph}),
\]
$\kappa$ is a homomorphism. By van Kampen's theorem
$\pi/\langle\!\langle m\rangle\!\rangle=\pi_1(\Sigma)=1$; as the image of $\kappa$ contains every
conjugate of $m$, $\kappa$ is surjective.

Let $\operatorname{As}(Q)$ act on $Q$ on the right by $x\cdot e_y=x*y$. The defining
relations and induction on word length give $w^{-1}e_xw=e_{x\cdot w}$ for all
$w\in\operatorname{As}(Q)$ and $x\in Q$. Because $Pg*Ph=Pg\cdot\kappa(e_{Ph})$, this action
is the composite of $\kappa$ with the action of $\pi$ on $P\backslash\pi$ by
right multiplication. Hence every $w\in\mathcal K:=\ker\kappa$ fixes $Q$
pointwise and therefore commutes with every $e_x$; thus $\mathcal K$ is
central.

The right multiplications by the conjugates of $m$ generate the action of
$\langle\!\langle m\rangle\!\rangle=\pi$, which is transitive on $P\backslash\pi$, so $Q$ is connected.
Hence all $e_x$ are conjugate in $\operatorname{As}(Q)$, and $\operatorname{As}(Q)^{\mathrm{ab}}$ is
infinite cyclic, generated by the class of any $e_x$; the assignment
$e_x\mapsto1$ defines an epimorphism onto $\mathbb Z$. Alexander duality in the
homology four-sphere $\Sigma$ (the proof of \cite[Theorem~3.44]{Hatcher}
uses only the homology of the ambient sphere) gives $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$,
generated by the class of $m=\kappa(e_P)$, and
$H_2(X;\mathbb Z)\cong\widetilde H^1(S^2;\mathbb Z)=0$. Hence $\kappa$ induces an
isomorphism on abelianizations, and $\mathcal K\subseteq[\operatorname{As}(Q),\operatorname{As}(Q)]$.

The five-term exact sequence in group homology for the central extension
\cite[p.~47]{Brown1982}
$1\to\mathcal K\to\operatorname{As}(Q)\to\pi\to1$ reads
\[
 H_2(\operatorname{As}(Q);\mathbb Z)\to H_2(\pi;\mathbb Z)\to\mathcal K\to
 H_1(\operatorname{As}(Q);\mathbb Z)\to H_1(\pi;\mathbb Z)\to0,
\]
where $\mathcal K/[\mathcal K,\operatorname{As}(Q)]=\mathcal K$ because $\mathcal K$ is
central. The fourth map is injective, so $\mathcal K$ is a quotient of
$H_2(\pi;\mathbb Z)$. By Hopf's theorem \cite[Chapter~II]{Brown1982},
$H_2(\pi;\mathbb Z)$ is a quotient of
$H_2(X;\mathbb Z)=0$. Thus $\mathcal K=1$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:As-algebraic}
The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:As-twoknot} uses the knot only through three
properties of the marked group $(\pi,m)$: $m$ normally generates $\pi$,
$\pi^{\mathrm{ab}}$ is infinite cyclic generated by the class of $m$, and
$H_2(\pi;\mathbb Z)=0$. For $(G_7,t)$ the first two are
Lemma~\ref{lem:group-data}. For the third, apply the Wang sequence
\cite[Example~2.48]{Hatcher} to the mapping torus of a self-homotopy
equivalence of $B\Gamma$ inducing $\theta$. This mapping torus is a
classifying space for $G_7=\Gamma\rtimes_\theta\langle t\rangle$, and its
homology sequence contains the exact segment
\[
 H_2(\Gamma;\mathbb Z)\to H_2(G_7;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(\Gamma;\mathbb Z)
 \xrightarrow{\;1-\theta_*\;}H_1(\Gamma;\mathbb Z).
\]
Here $H_2(\Gamma;\mathbb Z)=0$, since the Schur multipliers of $Q_8$ and $C_7$
vanish and $Q_8^{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes C_7=0$; here we use the standard
direct-product formula for Schur multipliers \cite{Karpilovsky1987}. On
$H_1(\Gamma;\mathbb Z)\cong(\mathbb Z/2)^2\oplus\mathbb Z/7$, with basis $\bar i,\bar j$ of the
first summand, $1-\theta_*$ is given by
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, of
determinant $-1$, on $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$ and by multiplication by $2$ on $\mathbb Z/7$.
Hence it is injective, and $H_2(G_7;\mathbb Z)=0$. Applied to the coset quandle
\eqref{eq:coset}, the argument shows algebraically that $e_x\mapsto x^{-1}tx$
is an isomorphism $\operatorname{As}(P_7)\to G_7$; the coset enumeration of
Remark~\ref{rem:As-direct} is an independent check. Consequently, for every
smooth oriented two-knot $K$ in a smooth homotopy four-sphere $\Sigma$ and
every quandle isomorphism $\psi\colon Q(\Sigma,K)\to P_7$, the composite
$\pi_1(X)\xrightarrow{\kappa^{-1}}\operatorname{As}(Q(\Sigma,K))\xrightarrow{\psi_*}
\operatorname{As}(P_7)\to G_7$ is an isomorphism carrying the meridian $g^{-1}mg$ to
$x^{-1}tx$ with $x=\psi(Pg)\in\Gamma$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:weight-loops}
The positive degree-one elements of $G_7$ form exactly two conjugacy
classes, represented by $t$ and $(-1)t$. Every such element normally generates
$G_7$. Every embedded loop representing such an element is ambiently
isotopic to a section of $M_7\to S^1$. The orientation-preserving
involution
$
                         \Phi[v,s]=[vi,s]
$
interchanges the two conjugacy classes. Consequently every framed
surgery on a loop of degree $\pm1$ in $M_7$ is represented by one of the pairs
in \eqref{eq:candidates}, up to the orientation of the belt sphere.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
This is \cite[Lemma~18.2 and Proposition~18.4(ii), pp.~356--359]{QextC}
specialized to $n=7$ and to the conventions of \eqref{eq:group} and
\eqref{per:eq:torus}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
\emph{Conjugacy classes.} The elements of degree one are the products $xt$
with $x\in\Gamma$. For $y\in\Gamma$, the convention \eqref{eq:group} gives
\[
 y^{-1}(xt)\,y=y^{-1}x\,\theta^{-1}(y)\,t,
 \;\;\;
 t^{-1}(xt)\,t=\theta(x)\,t .
\]
Taking $y=\theta(x)^{-1}$ in the first formula shows that $\theta(x)t$ is
$\Gamma$-conjugate to $xt$ (indeed, for this $y$ one has
$y^{-1}x\,\theta^{-1}(y)=\theta(x)\,x\,x^{-1}=\theta(x)$). Thus conjugation by the stable letter does not
enlarge a twisted-conjugacy orbit. Hence the conjugacy classes in $\Gamma t$ correspond to the orbits of
the twisted conjugation
$x\mapsto y^{-1}x\,\theta^{-1}(y)$ of $\Gamma$ on itself. Since $\theta^{-1}=\alpha^{-1}\times(c\mapsto c^{-1})$,
these orbits are products of orbits in the two factors. In $C_7$ the orbit
of $c^b$ is $\{c^{b-2a}\}=C_7$. In $Q_8$, the element $y^{-1}\alpha^{-1}(y)$
equals $1$, $j$, $k$ and $i$ for $y=\pm1$, $\pm i$, $\pm j$ and $\pm k$,
respectively, so the orbit of $1$ is $\{1,i,j,k\}$; multiplying by the
central element $-1$ shows that $\{-1,-i,-j,-k\}$ is the orbit of $-1$. Therefore the elements of positive degree one form exactly two
conjugacy classes,
\[
 \{1,i,j,k\}\times C_7\cdot t
 \;\;\text{and}\;\;
 \{-1,-i,-j,-k\}\times C_7\cdot t ,
\]
with twenty-eight elements each, represented by $t$ and $(-1)t$.

\emph{Normal generation.} Let $w$ have degree one. In $G_7/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle$ the
image of $t$ lies in the image of $\Gamma$, so this quotient is a quotient
of $\Gamma$. Its abelianization is a quotient of
$G_7^{\mathrm{ab}}/\langle[w]\rangle=0$. Thus $G_7/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle$ is a perfect
quotient of the solvable group $\Gamma$, and hence it is trivial.

\emph{The involution.} The map $\widetilde\Phi(v,s)=(vi,s)$ of
$S^3\times\mathbb R$ commutes with every $\gamma_{q,a}$, because $i$ commutes
with $\zeta$. Since $f^{-1}(w)=\omega wj^{-1}$ and $i^{-1}j^{-1}i=j$,
\[
 \widetilde\Phi D\widetilde\Phi^{-1}(v,s)
 =\bigl(\omega v\,i^{-1}j^{-1}i,\;s+1\bigr)
 =(\omega vj,\;s+1)
 =\gamma_{-1,0}D(v,s).
\]
Hence $\widetilde\Phi$ normalizes the deck group and descends to a
diffeomorphism $\Phi$ of $M_7$, which preserves $p$ and the orientation.
Moreover $\Phi^2=\mathrm{id}$, because $\widetilde\Phi^{2}=\gamma_{-1,0}$.
On $\pi_1(M_7)=G_7$, conjugation by $\widetilde\Phi$ induces the
automorphism that fixes $\Gamma$ pointwise and sends $t$ to $(-1)t$; it respects the
relation $t^{-1}gt=\theta(g)$ because $-1$ is central. Up to an inner
automorphism this is $\Phi_*$, so $\Phi$ interchanges the two conjugacy
classes.

\emph{Isotopy to a section.} Freely homotopic oriented embedded circles
in a smooth four-manifold are ambiently isotopic, by the unframed
circle-isotopy assertion of Lemma~\ref{lem:circle-spin}; its
transversality and isotopy-extension proof is given there.
This codimension-three observation was used directly for sections and
section surgeries of fibred two-knots by Teragaito
\cite{Teragaito1989Addendum}.
The section $\gamma$ represents $t$, and the section $\Phi\circ\gamma$
represents $(-1)t$.

\emph{Framed surgeries.} Reversing the orientation of a loop of degree
$-1$ changes only the orientation of the belt sphere. A loop of degree one
is ambiently isotopic to $\gamma$ or to $\Phi\circ\gamma$; in the second
case apply $\Phi$. The isotopy and $\Phi$ carry the given framing to one of
the two framing classes $\lambda_\pm$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:frame}, and framed
surgery depends only on the isotopy class of the framed circle. Hence the
result is diffeomorphic as a pair to $(\Sigma_+(7),K_+)$ or to
$(\Sigma_-(7),K_-)$, up to the orientation of the belt sphere.

\emph{Framings of the opposite orientation class.} Lemma~\ref{lem:frame}
classifies the framings of $\gamma$ that induce on its normal bundle the
same orientation as $\lambda_+$, and the preceding paragraph applies to
framings of this kind. A framing inducing the opposite orientation occurs,
for example, after the orientation of a loop of degree $-1$ is reversed,
which reverses the normal orientation induced from the loop and from $M_7$.
It also occurs after transport by an orientation-reversing diffeomorphism,
as in Remark~\ref{rem:rigidity-outline}(d). Such a framing is represented
by $T\circ(\mathrm{id}_{S^1}\times r)$, where $T$ is a tubular embedding
representing $\lambda_+$ or $\lambda_-$ and $r=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1)$. With
attaching maps $\phi_T(x,e^{2\pi is})=T(s,x)$ as in
Section~\ref{sec:construction},
\[
 \phi_{T\circ(\mathrm{id}\times r)}=\phi_T\circ\bigl(r|_{S^2}\times\mathrm{id}_{S^1}\bigr).
\]
Since $r|_{S^2}\times\mathrm{id}_{D^2}$ extends $r|_{S^2}\times\mathrm{id}_{S^1}$ over
$S^2\times D^2$, the identity of $M_7\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu\gamma$ together with
$r|_{S^2}\times\mathrm{id}_{D^2}$ is a diffeomorphism between the two surgered
manifolds. It carries belt sphere onto belt sphere and reverses the
orientation of the latter. Hence every framing of a loop of degree $\pm1$
yields $(\Sigma_+(7),K_+)$ or $(\Sigma_-(7),K_-)$ up to the orientation of
the belt sphere.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:two-classes}
The two positive degree-one conjugacy classes are represented by $t$ and
$(-1)t$ and are interchanged by the involution $\Phi$; see
\cite[Lemma~18.2(i),(iii), pp.~356--358]{QextC}. Thus there are two conjugacy
classes but one positive strict weight orbit. This distinction is the only
weight-class information used below.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:rigidity}
Every smooth oriented fibred two-knot with quandle $P_7$ in a smooth
homotopy four-sphere determines a pair diffeomorphic, possibly after reversing
the knot orientation, to one of the pairs
\[
                     (\Sigma_+(7),K_+),\;\;\;(\Sigma_-(7),K_-).
\]
Thus there are at most two types under equivalence that permits reversal of
the knot orientation.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
This is the case $n=7$ of \cite[Theorem~18.5(iii), pp.~359--360]{QextC}.

Independently of \cite{QextC}, Remark~\ref{rem:rigidity-outline} below
gives a complete proof within the present paper. Apart from standard
differential topology and the coset description of the fundamental
quandle \cite{Joyce,WinterHigher}, its only external inputs are
Perelman's elliptization theorem
\cite{PerelmanEntropy,PerelmanSurg,PerelmanExt}, used in step~(b), and
the fact that every diffeomorphism of $N_7$ is isotopic to an isometry
\cite[Theorem~1.2.1]{HKMR2012}, used in step~(c). The algebraic and
fibrewise steps rest on Lemma~\ref{lem:As-twoknot},
Remark~\ref{rem:As-algebraic}, the self-contained verification of
Lemma~\ref{lem:weight-loops} and the circle-isotopy statement of
Lemma~\ref{lem:circle-spin}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:rigidity-outline}
For the reader's convenience we indicate how Theorem~\ref{thm:rigidity}
follows from the material above. Besides the knot--quandle dictionary of
Section~\ref{sec:construction}, the argument uses Perelman's elliptization
theorem \cite{PerelmanEntropy,PerelmanSurg,PerelmanExt} and the
generalized Smale conjecture, which holds for all prism and quaternionic
manifolds \cite{HKMR2012}, in particular for $N_7$. Let $K\subset\Sigma$ be
a smooth oriented fibred two-knot with $Q(\Sigma,K)\cong P_7$, exterior
$X$, fibre $F$ and closed monodromy $\hat h$.

(a) \emph{Group and fibre.} By the dictionary and
Proposition~\ref{prop:exists}, $\pi_1(X)\cong\operatorname{As}(P_7)\cong G_7$, and
meridians correspond to conjugates of $t$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:As-twoknot} and Remark~\ref{rem:As-algebraic} prove this
step for an arbitrary smooth oriented two-knot in a smooth homotopy
four-sphere: any quandle isomorphism $Q(\Sigma,K)\cong P_7$ induces an
isomorphism $\pi_1(X)\cong G_7$ that carries each meridian to an element
$x^{-1}tx$ with $x\in\Gamma$.
The bundle projection induces an
epimorphism $\pi_1(X)\to\mathbb Z$ that sends a meridian to $1$, hence the degree
homomorphism. The exact homotopy sequence of the bundle identifies
$\pi_1(F)=\pi_1(\widehat F)$ with its kernel $\Gamma$, and under this
identification $\hat h$ induces the outer class of conjugation by a
meridian, namely $[\theta]$.

(b) \emph{The closed fibre is $N_7$.} By elliptization,
$\widehat F=S^3/\rho(\Gamma)$ for a free orthogonal action $\rho$, which is
orientation-preserving because $\widehat F$ is orientable. Write the elements
of $SO(4)=(S^3\times S^3)/\{\pm(1,1)\}$ as
$[(x,y)]\colon v\mapsto xvy^{-1}$. The unique involution $-1$ of $\Gamma$
acts by $-\mathrm{id}=[(-1,1)]$, the only free involution in $SO(4)$. If
$q\in\{\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ and $\rho(q)=[(x,y)]$, then
$(x^2,y^2)=\pm(-1,1)$, so $\rho(q)$ has the form $[(x,1)]$ or $[(1,y)]$.
Elements of these two forms commute, whereas $\rho(i)$ commutes neither with
$\rho(j)$ nor with $\rho(k)$. Hence, after conjugating, if necessary, by the
orientation-reversing isometry $v\mapsto\bar v$, which exchanges the two
factors, $\rho(Q_8)$ acts by left multiplication by a subgroup of $S^3$
isomorphic to $Q_8$, and such a subgroup is conjugate to the standard
$Q_8$. If $\rho(c)=[(x,y)]$, then commutation with $\rho(Q_8)$ forces
$x=\pm1$, so $\rho(c)$ is right multiplication by an element of order
seven. After a further conjugation in $SO(4)$ and an automorphism of
$\Gamma$, the action $\rho$ becomes \eqref{eq:action}. Thus $\widehat F$ is
diffeomorphic to $N_7$, possibly reversing orientation.

(c) \emph{The closed monodromy.}
Since $X$ is orientable, $\hat h$ preserves the orientation of
$\widehat F$: the mapping torus of an orientation-reversing diffeomorphism
of a connected orientable manifold is nonorientable. Conjugating by a
diffeomorphism $\widehat F\toN_7$, whether or not it preserves orientation,
therefore gives an element of $\operatorname{Diff}^+(N_7)$, to which the injectivity
statement below applies.
Transport $\hat h$ to $N_7$ by such a
diffeomorphism. Its outer class changes by an automorphism of $\Gamma$.
Since $\operatorname{Out}(\Gamma)=\operatorname{Out}(Q_8)\times\operatorname{Aut}(C_7)$ and $[\theta]=([\alpha],-1)$,
the transported class is $([\alpha]^{\pm1},-1)$, the class of
$\bar f^{\pm1}$. Every orientation-preserving isometry of $N_7$ is induced
by a map $v\mapsto AvB$ in which $A$ lies in the normalizer of $Q_8$ in
$S^3$, the binary octahedral group, and
$B\in\{e^{i\phi}\}\cup j\{e^{i\phi}\}$. Such a map induces the trivial outer
automorphism exactly when $A\in Q_8$ and $B\in\{e^{i\phi}\}$, and it then
lies in the identity component $\{[v\mapsto ve^{i\phi}]\}$ of
$\operatorname{Isom}^+(N_7)$. Hence $\pi_0\operatorname{Isom}^+(N_7)\to\operatorname{Out}(\Gamma)$ is injective. By the
Smale conjecture for $N_7$ (only its $\pi_0$-part \cite[Theorem~1.2.1]{HKMR2012} is used here; in
the terminology of \cite[Section~1.1, Table~1]{HKMR2012}, $N_7$ is a
quaternionic manifold, so the full conjecture
\cite[Theorem~1.2.2]{HKMR2012} also applies), the same holds for $\pi_0\operatorname{Diff}^+(N_7)$, so the
transported closed monodromy is isotopic to $\bar f$ or to $\bar f^{-1}$.

(d) \emph{Reconstruction.} Cap each fibre of $X$ by a ball, that is, form
$\widehat X=X\cup_{\partial}(D^3\times S^1)$. Then $\widehat X$ is the
mapping torus of $\hat h$, so it is diffeomorphic to $M_7$ by (b) and (c);
the mapping torus of $\bar f^{-1}$ is $M_7$ with the base direction
reversed. The pair $(\Sigma,K)$ is recovered from $\widehat X$ by framed
surgery on the core circle $\{0\}\times S^1$, whose belt sphere is $K$. This
circle is a section of $\widehat X\to S^1$, so it has degree $\pm1$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:weight-loops} identifies $(\Sigma,K)$, up to the orientation
of $K$, with $(\Sigma_+(7),K_+)$ or with $(\Sigma_-(7),K_-)$.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{per:lem:rigidity}
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ and $E$ be unit quaternions. Then $AvB=CvE$ for all $v\in S^3$ if
and only if $(C,E)=(\epsilon A,\epsilon B)$ for some $\epsilon=\pm1$.
Moreover the isometry $v\mapsto AvB$ of $S^3$ has a fixed point if and
only if
\begin{equation}\label{per:eq:fixcrit}
                     \operatorname{Re}(A)=\operatorname{Re}(B).
\end{equation}
When a fixed point exists and $A\neq\pm1$, the fixed-point set is a great circle.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
These are standard consequences of the unit-quaternion description of
$SO(4)$; see \cite{DuVal1964,ConwaySmith2003} and
\cite[Section~2]{MecchiaSeppi2015}. In the convention used here, the
only pairs acting trivially by $v\mapsto AvB$ are $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$.
If $AvB=CvE$ for all $v$, then
$\lambda:=C^{-1}A=EB^{-1}$
satisfies $\lambda v=v\lambda$ for all $v\in S^3$, so $\lambda=\pm1$; the
converse is clear. Next, $AvB=v$ is equivalent to $v^{-1}Av=B^{-1}$; two
unit quaternions are conjugate in $S^3$ exactly when their real parts agree,
and $\operatorname{Re}(B^{-1})=\operatorname{Re}(\overline B)=\operatorname{Re}(B)$, which gives
\eqref{per:eq:fixcrit}. The solution set is a coset of the centralizer of
$A$, which is a great circle for $A\neq\pm1$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{per:thm:periodic}
With the data of Section~\ref{sec:construction} and \eqref{per:eq:torus}, the following statements hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $f^n(v)=\omega^{-n}vj^n$ for all $n$, and
      $f^6=\gamma_{-1,0}$, that is, $f^6(v)=-v$. Moreover $f$ has
      order $12$ in $\operatorname{Isom}(S^3)$.
\item $f^n\in\Gamma$ if and only if $6\mid n$. Hence, the closed
      monodromy $\bar f$ has order exactly six in $\operatorname{Diff}(N_7)$,
      and $\theta$ has order exactly six in $\operatorname{Aut}(\Gamma)$.
\item $G_7$ acts freely, properly discontinuously, cocompactly and
      isometrically on $S^3\times\mathbb R$; thus $M_7$ is a closed
      four-manifold with the geometry $\mathbb S^3\times\mathbb E^1$, and
      it admits a metric of positive scalar curvature.
\item The subgroup $\Gamma\times\langle T\rangle$, where $T(v,s)=(v,s+6)$,
      equals $\langle\Gamma,D^6\rangle$ and has index six in $G_7$. The
      corresponding cover is canonically described by
      \begin{equation}\label{per:eq:sixfold}
       N_7\times S^1\toM_7,\;\;\;
       M_7=(N_7\times S^1)\big/\bigl\langle(\bar f^{-1},
             \text{rotation by }\tfrac{2\pi}{6})\bigr\rangle,
      \end{equation}
      where the $\mathbb Z/6$-action is free and $S^1=\mathbb R/6\mathbb Z$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Parts~(i), (ii) and the closed-monodromy component of~(iv) are the
$n=7$ specialization of \cite[Proposition~15.24, pp.~275--276]{QextC}; the
sixfold product cover and suspension description are
\cite[Proposition~21.2(iv), pp.~379--380]{QextC}. For~(iii), an element of nonzero base degree translates the $\mathbb R$
coordinate in \eqref{per:eq:torus}, whereas an element of degree zero
belongs to the freely acting finite group $\Gamma$.
Thus the action is free, proper and cocompact. The round product metric on
$S^3\times\mathbb R$ is invariant and has positive scalar curvature, so it
descends to $M_7$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Since $f(v)=\omega^{-1}vj$, induction gives $f^n(v)=\omega^{-n}vj^n$ for all
$n\in\mathbb Z$. As $\omega^3=1$ and $j^2=-1$, this gives $f^6(v)=-v$, that is,
$f^6=\gamma_{-1,0}$. By Lemma~\ref{per:lem:rigidity}, $f^n=\gamma_{q,a}$
holds exactly when $(\omega^{-n},j^n)=\pm(q,\zeta^{-a})$. The second
coordinate then lies in $\mathbb R+\mathbb R i$, which forces $j^n=\pm1$; hence $n$ is
even, $\zeta^{-a}=\pm1$, and $a=0$ because $\zeta$ has odd order. The first
coordinate then lies in $\pm Q_8=Q_8$, which forces $3\mid n$, because
$\omega$ and $\omega^2$ have real part $-\tfrac12$. Hence $f^n\in\Gamma$ if
and only if $6\mid n$, and $\bar f$ has order exactly six. The lifts of $\mathrm{id}_{N_7}$ to $S^3$ are precisely the deck transformations.
Thus $\bar f^{\,n}=\mathrm{id}_{N_7}$ if and only if $f^n\in\Gamma$. Similarly,
$f^n=\mathrm{id}$ exactly when $(\omega^{-n},j^n)=\pm(1,1)$; since
$-1\notin\langle\omega\rangle$, this means $\omega^{-n}=1=j^n$, that is,
$12\mid n$. Finally $\theta^n=\alpha^n\times(c\mapsto c^{(-1)^n})$, and
$\alpha$ has order three, so $\theta$ has order six.

For~(iv), $D^6(v,s)=(f^{-6}(v),s+6)=\gamma_{-1,0}T(v,s)$, and $T$ commutes
with every $\gamma_{q,a}$. Hence
$\langle\Gamma,D^6\rangle=\Gamma\times\langle T\rangle$. This subgroup is the
kernel of the base degree modulo six, so it is normal of index six. Its
quotient of $S^3\times\mathbb R$ is $N_7\times\mathbb R/6\mathbb Z$, on which $D$ induces
$([v],s)\mapsto(\bar f^{-1}[v],s+1)$. This map rotates the circle factor by
$2\pi/6$, so it generates a free $\mathbb Z/6$-action, and the quotient is $M_7$;
this is \eqref{per:eq:sixfold}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{per:prop:fixed}\label{nf:prop:fixed}
For $1\leq n\leq5$, the fixed-point set of $\bar f^{\,n}$ on $N_7$ is given by
\[
 \operatorname{Fix}(\bar f^{\,n})=\emptyset\;\;(n=1,2,4,5),\;\;\;
 \operatorname{Fix}(\bar f^{\,3})=\mathcal C_1\sqcup\mathcal C_2\sqcup\mathcal C_3,
\]
where the $\mathcal C_r$ are disjoint embedded geodesic circles. The
involution $\bar f^{\,3}$ fixes each $\mathcal C_r$ pointwise, and
$\bar f$ permutes the three circles cyclically. The preimage of
$\operatorname{Fix}(\bar f^{\,3})$ in $S^3$ is the union of the $42$ great circles
$\operatorname{Fix}(\gamma_{q,a}f^3)$ with $q\in\{\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ and
$a\in\mathbb Z/7$. The action of $\Gamma$ on this set of circles has three orbits
of size fourteen.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
For the fixed-point sets we use the quaternionic criterion of
Lemma~\ref{per:lem:rigidity}; compare
\cite[Propositions~15.24 and~21.2(iii)]{QextC}. A fixed point of $\bar f^{\,n}$ exists exactly when, for some
$q\in Q_8$ and $a\in\mathbb Z/7$, the equation
\[
       q^{-1}\omega^{-n}v j^n\zeta^a=v
\]
has a solution. By Lemma~\ref{per:lem:rigidity}, this is equivalent to
\[
       \operatorname{Re}(q^{-1}\omega^{-n})=\operatorname{Re}(j^n\zeta^a).
\]
For $n\in\{1,2,4,5\}$, the left-hand side is always $\pm\tfrac12$: the
element $q^{-1}\omega^{-n}$ lies in $Q_8\omega\cup Q_8\omega^2$, and these
sixteen elements of the binary tetrahedral group $\langle i,j,\omega\rangle$
are exactly the quaternions $\tfrac12(\pm1\pm i\pm j\pm k)$.
For $n=1,5$, the right-hand side is zero. For $n=2,4$, it is
$(-1)^{n/2}\cos(2\pi a/7)$, which cannot equal $\pm\tfrac12$: a unit
complex number with real part $\pm\tfrac12$ has order three or six,
whereas $\zeta^a$ has order dividing seven. Hence all four powers are
fixed-point free. It remains to count the components of the fixed set
of the third power.

A point $[v]\inN_7$ is fixed by $\bar f^{\,3}$ exactly when
$f^3(v)=\gamma_{q,a}(v)$ for some $(q,a)\in Q_8\times\mathbb Z/7$.
Equivalently,
$
        q^{-1}v\,j^3\zeta^a=v
$,
because $\omega^{-3}=1$. By Lemma~\ref{per:lem:rigidity}, this equation has
a solution exactly when
\[
        \operatorname{Re}(q^{-1})=\operatorname{Re}(j^3\zeta^a)=0,
\]
that is, precisely for
$q\in\{\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ and arbitrary $a\in\mathbb Z/7$. For each of
these $42$ choices, the corresponding isometry has a great circle as its fixed-point set.
Each of them is an involution, since $q^{-2}=-1=(j^3\zeta^a)^2$.
As $(q,a)$ ranges over these choices, the resulting circles form the same collection as the
$42$ circles $\operatorname{Fix}(\gamma_{q,a}f^3)$ appearing in the statement (inverting the
$\Gamma$-factor merely relabels the set of pairs).

Distinct elements of the coset $\Gamma f^3$ cannot fix a common point: their
quotient would be a nonidentity element of the freely acting deck group
$\Gamma$ fixing that point. Hence, these $42$ great circles are pairwise
disjoint. For $h\in\Gamma$ and $g\in\Gamma f^3$, one has
$h\,\operatorname{Fix}(g)=\operatorname{Fix}(hgh^{-1})$ with $hgh^{-1}\in\Gamma f^3$.
Hence if $h$ carries a point of $\operatorname{Fix}(g)$ into $\operatorname{Fix}(g')$ for some
$g'\in\Gamma f^3$, then $hgh^{-1}=g'$ by the preceding disjointness
argument. Thus only the stabilizer of a circle identifies points of that
circle, and circles in different $\Gamma$-orbits have disjoint images.
Conjugation by a deck transformation gives
\[
 \gamma_{p,b}(\gamma_{q,a}f^3)\gamma_{p,b}^{-1}
       =\gamma_{pqp^{-1},\,a+2b}f^3,
\]
because $f^3\gamma_{p,b}f^{-3}=\gamma_{p,-b}$. The first coordinate ranges
over the $Q_8$-conjugacy class $\{q,-q\}$ and the second over all of
$\mathbb Z/7$. Thus, the $42$ circles split into three $\Gamma$-orbits of size
$14$, indexed by the three axes $\{\pm i\}$, $\{\pm j\}$ and
$\{\pm k\}$. Their images are therefore three disjoint embedded geodesic
circles $\mathcal C_1$, $\mathcal C_2$ and $\mathcal C_3$ in $N_7$.

More explicitly, put $C_{q,a}=\operatorname{Fix}(\gamma_{q,a}f^3)$.
The disjointness of the fixed circles shows that the setwise stabilizer of this circle
is the centralizer of $\gamma_{q,a}f^3$ in $\Gamma$.
The displayed conjugation formula therefore gives
\[
 \operatorname{Stab}_{\Gamma}(C_{q,a})
 =\{\gamma_{p,0}:p\in C_{Q_8}(q)\}
 =\{\gamma_{p,0}:p\in\langle q\rangle\}
 \cong C_4.
\]
Indeed, $a+2b=a$ forces $b=0$ in $\mathbb Z/7$, and the centralizer
in $Q_8$ of a noncentral element $q$ is $\langle q\rangle$.
This agrees with the orbit count $56/14=4$.
This order-four stabilizer acts freely on $C_{q,a}$, since the
deck action is free. A circle isometry that reverses orientation has
a fixed point, so the stabilizer acts by rotations.
Thus each of the fourteen great circles in one $\Gamma$-orbit maps
with covering degree four onto its image in $N_7$.
Only the stabilizer identifies points of a given circle, and circles
in different $\Gamma$-orbits have disjoint images. Consequently
these images are embedded circles. Since $S^3\toN_7$ is a local
isometry, they are geodesic.

Finally,
$f\operatorname{Fix}(\gamma_{q,a}f^3)=\operatorname{Fix}(\gamma_{\alpha(q),-a}f^3)$ and $\alpha$ cycles
$i\mapsto j\mapsto k\mapsto i$, so $\bar f$ cyclically permutes the three
components. By construction $\bar f^3$ fixes each component pointwise. This
refines the exceptional-orbit description in
\cite[Proposition~21.2(iv), pp.~379--380]{QextC}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{per:thm:action}
Translations $T_r(v,s)=(v,s+r)$ along the $\mathbb R$-factor descend to a
smooth, effective action of $S^1=\mathbb R/6\mathbb Z$ on $M_7$ with the following
properties:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item The action has no fixed points. The isotropy group at $[v,s]$ is
      cyclic of order $6/k_0$, where
      $k_0=\min\{n>0:\bar f^{\,n}[v]=[v]\}$, and the orbit through
      $[v,s]$ has degree $k_0$ under $p_*$.
\item We have $k_0\in\{3,6\}$. Principal orbits have $k_0=6$; the exceptional
      orbits are those with $[v]\in\operatorname{Fix}(\bar f^{\,3})$; they have
      isotropy of order two and degree three, and their union is a single
      embedded torus
      \[
       \mathcal E=\bigl\{[v,s]:[v]\in\operatorname{Fix}(\bar f^{\,3})\bigr\}\cong T^2.
      \]
\item The class of a principal orbit is $(-1)t^{6}\in G_7$, which is
      central and has degree six.
\item $\Lambda$ has order $336$, and the orbit map realizes $M_7$ as a
      Seifert-fibred four-manifold over the spherical three-orbifold
      $
       M_7/S^1=N_7/\langle\bar f\rangle=S^3/\Lambda
      $,
      whose singular set is one circle with isotropy of order two.
\item There is a central extension
      \begin{equation}\label{per:eq:centralext}
       1\to\mathbb Z\bigl\langle(-1)t^{6}\bigr\rangle
        \to G_7\to\Lambda\to1.
      \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The effective period-six suspension action, the isotropy formula, and the
orbit-space identification with $N_7/\langle\bar f\rangle$ are precisely the
$n=7$ case of \cite[Proposition~21.2(iv), pp.~379--380]{QextC}. Together
with Proposition~\ref{per:prop:fixed}, this gives~(i) and shows that the
only exceptional orbits occur over $\operatorname{Fix}(\bar f^{\,3})$ with isotropy
$C_2$. Since $\bar f$ cyclically permutes the three components of
$\operatorname{Fix}(\bar f^{\,3})$ and $\bar f^{\,3}$ fixes them pointwise, their mapping
torus is a single torus $\mathcal E\cong T^2$, proving~(ii).

Equivalently, $\mathcal E=\operatorname{Fix}(T_3)$: by~(i), the time-three map fixes
$[v,s]$ exactly when $k_0\mid3$, that is, when $k_0=3$. Since $T_3$ is an
isometry of the metric induced by the round product metric on $S^3\times\mathbb R$
(Theorem~\ref{per:thm:periodic}(iii)), $\mathcal E$ is a closed totally
geodesic, in particular smoothly embedded, submanifold
\cite[Chapter~II]{Kobayashi1972}.

For~(iii), a principal orbit lifts from $(v_0,0)$ to $(v_0,6)$. Because
$f^{-6}=-\mathrm{id}$, the corresponding deck element is
$\gamma_{-1,0}D^6$, hence its class is $(-1)t^6$. This element is central:
$-1\in Z(\Gamma)$ is fixed by $\theta$, and $\theta^6=\mathrm{id}$.

For~(iv)--(v), the least positive power of $f$ contained in $\Gamma$ is
$f^6$, so $[\Lambda:\Gamma]=6$ and $|\Lambda|=336$. Projection to the
$S^3$-coordinate gives a surjection $G_7\to\Lambda$ with
\[
 \ker(G_7\to\Lambda)
 =\bigl\langle\gamma_{-1,0}D^6\bigr\rangle
 =\mathbb Z\bigl\langle(-1)t^6\bigr\rangle,
\]
which proves \eqref{per:eq:centralext}.

For the kernel, note that $\gamma_{q,a}D^n$ acts on the $S^3$-coordinate
by $\gamma_{q,a}f^{-n}$. If this map is the identity, then $f^n\in\Gamma$,
so $6\mid n$ by Theorem~\ref{per:thm:periodic}(ii); then
$f^{-n}=\gamma_{(-1)^{n/6},0}$ forces $(q,a)=((-1)^{n/6},0)$, and, since
$\gamma_{-1,0}$ commutes with $D$, the element is
$(\gamma_{-1,0}D^6)^{n/6}=T_n$. Conversely, $T_6=\gamma_{-1,0}D^6$ acts
trivially on the $S^3$-coordinate, and it has infinite order because it
translates the $\mathbb R$-coordinate by six. Its class $(-1)t^6$ is central
by~(iii). The orbit map is therefore
$M_7\to S^3/\Lambda$. Moreover $\mathcal E/S^1$ is a single circle. At a point
of this circle the time-three isotropy acts on a transverse
three-dimensional slice as an involution with one-dimensional fixed
subspace; in suitable coordinates it is
$(\xi,\eta)\mapsto(\xi,-\eta)$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2$. Hence the singular
locus has local group $C_2$, while principal orbits have the product local
model. This establishes the asserted Seifert fibration and the isomorphism
$\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(S^3/\Lambda)\cong\Lambda$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Each translation $T_r$ commutes with every $\gamma_{q,a}$ and with $D$, so it
descends to $M_7$, and $T_6=\gamma_{-1,0}D^6$ is a deck transformation by
Theorem~\ref{per:thm:periodic}(iv). Hence $\mathbb R/6\mathbb Z$ acts smoothly on $M_7$.
If $T_r[v,s]=[v,s]$, then $(v,s+r)=\gamma_{q,a}D^n(v,s)$ for some $(q,a)$
and some $n\in\mathbb Z$. Comparing $\mathbb R$-coordinates gives $r=n$, and then
$v=\gamma_{q,a}f^{-n}(v)$, that is, $\bar f^{\,n}[v]=[v]$. Conversely, if
$\bar f^{\,n}[v]=[v]$, then $T_n[v,s]=[v,s]$. Thus the isotropy group at $[v,s]$ is $k_0\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$, which is cyclic of order $6/k_0$; here $k_0\mid6$
because $\bar f^{\,6}=\mathrm{id}$. In particular every isotropy group is finite,
so there are no fixed points, and the orbit $r\mapsto[v,s+r]$,
$0\leq r\leq k_0$, has degree $k_0$ under $p_*$. By
Proposition~\ref{per:prop:fixed}, $k_0\notin\{1,2\}$; hence
$k_0\in\{3,6\}$, and $k_0=3$ exactly when $[v]\in\operatorname{Fix}(\bar f^{\,3})$. Points
outside the three circles $\mathcal C_1$, $\mathcal C_2$ and $\mathcal C_3$
have trivial isotropy, so the action is effective.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{per:rem:seifert-terminology}
In Theorem~\ref{per:thm:action}(iv), ``Seifert-fibred over the three-orbifold
$S^3/\Lambda$'' means that the orbit map of the fixed-point-free circle action is
an orbifold circle bundle, that is, a Seifert fibring with typical fibre $S^1$
in the sense of \cite{LeeRaymond2010}, as in Lemma~\ref{std:lem:exact}. This
differs from the four-dimensional usage of \cite[Section~7.7]{Hillman}, where a
Seifert-fibred four-manifold is the total space of an orbifold bundle with
general fibre a torus or a Klein bottle over a two-orbifold. By
\cite[Section~7.7]{Hillman} every $\mathbb S^3\times\mathbb E^1$-manifold, and
hence $M_7$, is also Seifert fibred in that sense; that structure is not used here.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{per:lem:gottlieb}
Let a path-connected topological group $G$ act continuously on a space $M$,
let $x\in M$, and define $\mathrm{ev}_x:G\to M$ by $g\mapsto g\cdot x$.
Then $(\mathrm{ev}_x)_*\pi_1(G,1)$ lies in the centre of $\pi_1(M,x)$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
This is the group-action case of Gottlieb's evaluation-subgroup
centrality theorem
\cite[Theorem~I.4 and the following paragraph, p.~843]{Gottlieb}.
Let $u:[0,1]\to G$ be a loop based at the identity
and let $\alpha:[0,1]\to M$ be a loop based at $x$.
The continuous map
\[
 H:[0,1]^2\to M,\;\;\; H(r,s)=u(r)\cdot\alpha(s)
\]
restricts to the boundary loop
$\beta*\alpha*\beta^{-1}*\alpha^{-1}$, where
$\beta(r)=u(r)\cdot x$.
The map $H$ fills this loop, so $[\beta]$ commutes with every $[\alpha]$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{fa:lem:orbit-surgery}
Let $X$ be a connected oriented smooth four-manifold with an effective
smooth circle action, and let $O\subset\operatorname{int} X$ be a circle orbit.
For either of its two oriented normal-framing classes, the action
extends to an effective smooth circle action on the manifold obtained
by surgery along $O$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
We give the local extension argument; for general background on
circle actions and equivariant modifications, see
\cite{FintushelSC,Fintushel1978,Pao}.
The isotropy of $O$ is a proper closed subgroup of $S^1$, so it is
$C_b$ for some $b\geq1$.
Choose an invariant Riemannian metric, obtained by averaging an arbitrary
metric over the circle \cite[Chapter~VI, Theorem~2.1]{Bredon}.
The equivariant tubular-neighbourhood theorem gives an invariant
neighbourhood equivariantly diffeomorphic to $S^1\times_{C_b}D^3$
\cite[Chapter~VI, Theorem~2.2 and Corollary~2.4,
pp.~306--309]{Bredon}.
The connected circle group preserves the orientation of $X$,
and its isotropy fixes the orbit pointwise because the group is
abelian. Hence the slice representation takes values in $SO(3)$.
It is faithful: an element in its kernel fixes the tube pointwise,
and an isometry equal to the identity on a nonempty open subset of
a connected manifold is the identity everywhere (the fixed-point set of an isometry is a closed totally geodesic submanifold
\cite[Chapter~II]{Kobayashi1972}, so a component containing a nonempty open
set is open and closed).
Thus a generator of $C_b$ acts on $D^3$ by a rotation
$R_{2\pi a/b}$ about an axis, with $\gcd(a,b)=1$.
When $b=1$, choose an arbitrary axis and take $a=0$.

Orient the normal bundle of $O$ so that the positive direction of $O$
followed by this normal orientation is the orientation of $X$. We identify
the slice with $\mathbb R^3$ by an orthonormal basis that is positively oriented
for this normal orientation and whose third vector spans the axis, and
$R_\theta$ denotes the rotation through the angle $\theta$ in the first two
coordinates. The two possible directions along the axis replace $a$ by
$-a$, which is immaterial below.

Here is an explicit product trivialization of this tube.
For $h=e^{2\pi i k/b}$ use the associated-bundle relation
\[
 (u,y)\sim(u h^{-1},R_{2\pi a k/b}y).
\]
The map
\[
 F_a:S^1\times_{C_b}D^3\to S^1\times D^3,\;\;\;
 F_a([e^{2\pi i s},y])
   =(e^{2\pi i b s},R_{2\pi a s}y)
\]
is well defined by that relation. Its inverse is obtained by choosing
a $b$th root of the first coordinate and undoing the indicated
rotation; the relation makes the inverse independent of this choice.
Local smooth choices of the root show that $F_a$ is a diffeomorphism.

The local coordinates $(s,y)\mapsto[e^{2\pi is},y]$ of the tube preserve
orientation by the convention fixed above, and in them the Jacobian matrix of
$F_a$ is block lower triangular, with diagonal blocks $b>0$ and
$R_{2\pi as}\in SO(3)$. Hence $F_a$ preserves orientation, and it is an
oriented framing of $O$; the same argument applies to $F_{a+b}$ below.
In these coordinates the circle action is
\begin{equation}\label{fa:eq:orbit-weights}
 t\cdot(z,y)=(e^{2\pi i b t}z,R_{2\pi a t}y),
 \;\;\; t\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z.
\end{equation}

For this framing, define the following action on the replacement
$S^2\times D^2$:
\[
             t\cdot(x,w)=(R_{2\pi a t}x,e^{2\pi i b t}w).
\]
Under the surgery identification
$(x,z)\in S^2\times\partial D^2\mapsto
(z,x)\in S^1\times\partial D^3$, its boundary action agrees with
\eqref{fa:eq:orbit-weights}.
Both actions preserve radial collar coordinates and are independent
of the collar parameter, so invariant product collars give a smooth
action on the manifold obtained by the oriented surgery.
Equivalently, the weighted formula extends over the surgery-trace
handle $D^2\times D^3$, and invariant rounding of its corners gives
the same extension.

The integer $a+b$ gives the same $C_b$ slice representation, and
the corresponding trivialization satisfies
\[
 F_{a+b}\circ F_a^{-1}(z,y)=(z,R_{\arg z}y).
\]
The full-rotation loop $z\mapsto R_{\arg z}$ represents the nonzero
class of $\pi_1(SO(3))\cong\mathbb Z/2$: its lift to the unit-quaternion
double cover starting at $1$ ends at $-1$.
The oriented normal bundle over the circle is trivial, and its
framing classes are classified by this group. Hence $F_a$ and
$F_{a+b}$ represent the two framing classes.
Replacing $a$ by $a+b$ in the action on the replacement piece therefore
performs the surgery with the other framing.
This weight change is the local form of the mechanism in Pao's argument
\cite{Pao}: after a Gluck twist along an invariant two-sphere, the circle
action on the exterior extends across the reglued piece with one rotation
weight changed by the other; see \cite[proof of Theorem~3.2]{FukudaGluck}, and
compare the equivariant disc-bundle constructions of \cite{FintushelSC}
summarized in \cite[Section~5.2]{GalazGarcia2012}.

For either choice, write $a'$ for the chosen weight, so
$a'\in\{a,a+b\}$ and $\gcd(a',b)=1$.
The extended action is effective already on the replacement piece:
if $t\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ acts trivially there, then $a't,bt\in\mathbb Z$,
and coprimality forces $t=0$ in $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$.
Its new fixed set consists of the two poles of $S^2\times\{0\}$ when
$a'\neq0$, and is all of $S^2\times\{0\}$ when $a'=0$.
These fixed points are allowed by
Remark~\ref{fa:rem:Pao}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{fa:rem:Pao}
A closed simply connected smooth four-manifold admitting an effective
smooth circle action is diffeomorphic to a connected sum of copies of
$S^4$, $\pm\mathbb {CP}^2$, and $S^2\times S^2$; see
\cite[Section~5.1, Theorem~5.1]{GalazGarcia2012}, based on the
classification of Fintushel and Pao \cite{Fintushel1978,Pao}. Consequently,
a smooth homotopy four-sphere with an effective smooth circle action is
diffeomorphic to $S^4$. No restriction on the fixed-point set is required.
As recorded in \cite[Section~5.1]{GalazGarcia2012}, this smooth statement
combines Fintushel's classification \cite{FintushelSC,Fintushel1978} and the
work of Pao \cite{Pao} with Perelman's proof of the three-dimensional
Poincar\'e conjecture \cite{PerelmanEntropy,PerelmanSurg,PerelmanExt}.
The validity of Fintushel's classification in the smooth category is
attributed there to \cite{FintushelSternSunukjian2009}.
Fintushel's identification of the four-manifold was originally established
modulo that conjecture, which enters through the simply connected
three-dimensional orbit space.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{per:thm:tower}
For every $m\geq1$ and either framing, $\Sigma^{(m)}_\varepsilon$ is a closed
smooth oriented four-manifold with $\chi=2$ and
\begin{equation}\label{per:eq:towergroups}
 \pi_1\bigl(\Sigma^{(m)}_\varepsilon\bigr)\cong
 \begin{cases}
  1, & m\equiv1,5\pmod 6,\\
  C_7, & m\equiv2,4\pmod 6,\\
  Q_8, & m\equiv3\pmod 6,\\
  \Gamma=Q_8\times C_7, & m\equiv0\pmod 6.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Consequently $b_1=b_2=0$ in every case, each $\Sigma^{(m)}_\varepsilon$ is a
rational homology four-sphere, and
$H_2(\Sigma^{(m)}_\varepsilon;\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(\Sigma^{(m)}_\varepsilon;\mathbb Z)
\cong\pi_1(\Sigma^{(m)}_\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{ab}}$. For
$m\equiv\pm1\pmod 6$ the cover $\Sigma^{(m)}_\varepsilon$ is itself a smooth
homotopy four-sphere.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
This is the parameter-seven specialization of
\cite[Proposition~20.1 and Remark~20.3, pp.~374--377]{QextC}. The statement
is independent of the framing label.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let $E^{(m)}\toE_7$ be the $m$-fold cyclic covering corresponding to the
subgroup $\Gamma\rtimes\langle t^m\rangle$ of elements whose degree is
divisible by $m$. The branched cover is
$\Sigma^{(m)}_\varepsilon=E^{(m)}\cup(S^2\times D^2)$, attached along the lift of
$\phi_\varepsilon$ through $(x,z)\mapsto(x,z^m)$; compare
\eqref{nf:eq:lifted-surgery} below. Hence
\[
 \chi\bigl(\Sigma^{(m)}_\varepsilon\bigr)
 =m\,\chi(E_7)+\chi(S^2\times D^2)-\chi(S^2\times S^1)=2 .
\]
The circle $\{x\}\times\partial D^2$ of the cap represents a conjugate of
$t^m$. Since $t^{-m}gt^m=\theta^m(g)$ for $g\in\Gamma$, killing $t^m$ imposes
exactly the relations $g=\theta^m(g)$, and van Kampen's theorem gives
\[
 \pi_1\bigl(\Sigma^{(m)}_\varepsilon\bigr)
 \cong(\Gamma\rtimes\langle t^m\rangle)/\langle\!\langle t^m\rangle\!\rangle
 \cong\Gamma/N_m,\;\;\;
 N_m=\bigl\langle g^{-1}\theta^m(g)\bigm| g\in\Gamma\bigr\rangle ;
\]
the subgroup $N_m$ is normal, since, as observed in
Definition~\ref{def:weight}, the subgroup generated by the elements
$g^{-1}\varphi(g)$ is normal for every automorphism $\varphi$.
For $g=(q,c^a)$ one has
$g^{-1}\theta^m(g)=\bigl(q^{-1}\alpha^m(q),\,c^{((-1)^m-1)a}\bigr)$. Taking
$g=(q,1)$ and $g=(1,c^a)$ shows that $N_m=A_m\times B_m$, where $A_m$ is
generated by the elements $q^{-1}\alpha^m(q)$ and $B_m$ by the elements
$c^{((-1)^m-1)a}$. If $3\nmid m$, then $\alpha^m\in\{\alpha,\alpha^2\}$, and
$q=i,j$ give two elements of $\{\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ on different axes
(namely $-k,-i$ or $j,k$), which generate $Q_8$; if $3\mid m$, then
$A_m=1$. Moreover $B_m=C_7$ for odd $m$, because $2$ is invertible modulo
$7$, and $B_m=1$ for even $m$. Hence $N_m$ equals $\Gamma$, $Q_8$, $C_7$ or
$1$ for $m\equiv\pm1$, $\pm2$, $3$ or $0$ modulo six, which gives
\eqref{per:eq:towergroups}. Since $\pi_1$ is finite, $b_1=b_3=0$, and
$\chi=2$ forces $b_2=0$. The identification $H_2\cong H_1$ is explained
below. For $m\equiv\pm1\pmod6$, the manifold $\Sigma^{(m)}_\varepsilon$ is simply
connected with $\chi=2$, so the argument of Section~\ref{sec:construction}
shows that it is a homotopy four-sphere.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{nf:lem:calibration}
Set $\eta_+=0$ and $\eta_-=1$. Then
\[
 \operatorname{sp}_{s_m}(\gamma_m,\lambda_{\varepsilon,m})
       =(-1)^{m\eta_\varepsilon}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Shearing the tangent vector of $\gamma$ to the base direction does not
change the closing sign: the vertical vectors $V_a(s)$, together with any
vector of positive base component, form a positively oriented frame, and
$\widetilde c$ is stationary near the seam, so the shear is a homotopy of
closed loops of oriented frames. Put $u_+:=u$, and let $u_-$ be as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:frame}. At $(\widetilde c(s),s)$ the trivialization
\eqref{nf:eq:trivialization} sends the base direction to $\widetilde c(s)$
and $V_a(s)$ to $\widetilde c(s)u_\varepsilon(s)\,a\,u_\varepsilon(s)^{-1}$, so
the full frame is the image of the basis $(1,i,j,k)$ under
$x\mapsto\widetilde c(s)u_\varepsilon(s)\,x\,u_\varepsilon(s)^{-1}$. It
therefore lifts to the path
\[
 (\widetilde c(s)u_\varepsilon(s),u_\varepsilon(s))\in\operatorname{Spin}(4).
\]
For the $+$ frame this path starts at $(f(1),1)$ and ends at $(j,j)$.
Since $\omega f(1)=j$, the endpoint is
\[
 (j,j)=d_1(f(1),1).
\]
Thus, the lift closes in the spin bundle of $M_1$, giving the sign $+1$.
For the $-$ frame the endpoint is $(-j,-j)=\kappa(j,j)$, giving the sign
$-1$. The lifted circle in the degree-$m$ cover traverses the original
framed loop $m$ times. Pulling back its two-sheeted spin-frame cover
raises the closing sign to the $m$th power, proving the formula.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:circle-spin}
Freely homotopic oriented embedded circles in a smooth oriented
four-manifold are ambiently isotopic. On a spin four-manifold $(W,s)$,
the spin structure extends across surgery on a framed circle $(C,\lambda)$
precisely when $\operatorname{sp}_s(C,\lambda)=-1$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
The circle-isotopy assertion is the standard codimension-three
observation used for sections of fibred two-knots in
\cite{Teragaito1989Addendum}. We give the general argument here, including
the relative transversality details needed in the earlier section-surgery
comparison.

Choose parametrizations of the two oriented circles and a smooth free
homotopy $H:S^1\times I\to W$ between them that is stationary near the ends.
Relative parametric transversality \cite[Chapter~3]{Hirsch} permits a
perturbation, fixed near the ends, such that $d(H_t)_z\neq0$ for every
$(z,t)$: the zero-derivative condition has codimension four in a
two-dimensional parameter space. The same perturbation can make the map
$
 (z,z',t)\longmapsto\bigl(H_t(z),H_t(z')\bigr),\;\;\; z\neq z',
$
transverse to the diagonal in $W\times W$. That diagonal has codimension
four and this parameter space has dimension three, so its preimage is
empty. Near $z=z'$, uniform local injectivity follows from the immersion
condition and compactness of $S^1\times I$; pairs away from the diagonal
are covered by the preceding multijet-transversality argument.
Each $H_t$ is therefore an injective immersion of the compact
circle, hence an embedding. The resulting smooth isotopy extends to an
ambient isotopy \cite[Chapter~8]{Hirsch}.

The trace of surgery on $(C,\lambda)$ is obtained by attaching a five-dimensional
two-handle $D^2\times D^3$ to $W\times I$. The normal framing allows us to
express the obstruction to extending the spin structure over that handle
in terms of
the spin structure induced on its attaching circle
\cite[Sections~5.6--5.7]{GS}. Extension holds precisely when this circle
has the bounding spin structure. For an oriented disc, the boundary tangent vector together with the inward
radial vector makes one full rotation in the disc plane. Stabilizing by
constant transverse vectors still gives a spin lift that does not close. Thus
the bounding structure has the closing sign
$-1$, proving the criterion. Equivalently, the spin structure on the
unchanged exterior extends over the surgery cap exactly under this
condition.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{wh:prop:product}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item The groups in the construction are full products:
      \[
       \Gamma=Q_8\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}} C_{14},\;\;\;
       \Lambda=T^{*}\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}}Q_{28}.
      \]
      Their orders are $56$ and $336$, respectively.
\item $[\Lambda,\Lambda]=\Gamma$ and $\Lambda^{\mathrm{ab}}=\Lambda/\Gamma$
      is cyclic of order six, generated by the image of $f$.
\item The index-two subgroup $\Lambda^+:=T^{*}\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}} C_{14}$ acts freely on
      $S^3$, and $\Lambda^+\congT^{*}\times C_7$.
\item The nontrivial elements of $\Lambda$ with a fixed point are the $42$
      involutions $(A,B)$ with $A\in\{\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ and
      $B\in\{\pm\zeta^mj\}$; they lie in the coset $f^3\Gamma$, and none
      of them lies in $\Lambda^+$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
(i) The generators $\gamma_{q,a}=(q,\zeta^{-a})$ and $f=(\omega^{-1},j)$ lie
in $T^{*}\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}}Q_{28}$. This group has order $24\cdot28/2=336=|\Lambda|$
(Theorem~\ref{per:thm:action}(iv)), so the inclusion is an equality. In the
same way, $\Gamma\subseteq Q_8\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}} C_{14}$, and both groups have order $56$.
Since $\omega^3=1$, we have $f^3=(1,j^3)=(1,-j)$.

(ii) The group $\Gamma$ is normal and $\Lambda/\Gamma$ is cyclic of order
six, generated by $f$ (Theorem~\ref{per:thm:periodic}(ii)). Hence
$[\Lambda,\Lambda]\subseteq\Gamma$. Conversely, $[T^{*},T^{*}]=Q_8$, and
$(1,\zeta)$ and $(1,j)$ have commutator $(1,\zeta^{\pm2})$. So
$[\Lambda,\Lambda]$ contains $Q_8\times1$ and $1\times C_7$, which together
generate $\Gamma$; note that $(1,-1)=(-1,1)$.

(iii) By Lemma~\ref{per:lem:rigidity}, $(A,B)$ has a fixed point exactly
when $\operatorname{Re} A=\operatorname{Re} B$. For $A\inT^{*}$ we have $\operatorname{Re} A\in\{0,\pm\frac12,\pm1\}$.
For $B\in C_{14}$ we have $\operatorname{Re} B\in\{\pm\cos(\pi m/7)\}$. These sets meet
only in $\pm1$, which gives the identity. The map
$T^{*}\times C_7\to\Lambda^+$ given by $(A,c)\mapsto(A,c)$ is injective because
$C_7$ has odd order. The two groups have the same order.

(iv) For $B\inQ_{28}\setminus C_{14}=\{\pm\zeta^mj\}$ we have $\operatorname{Re} B=0$, so
$(A,B)$ has a fixed point exactly when $A$ is one of the six elements of
order four in $T^{*}$. Then $(A,B)^2=(-1,-1)$ is the identity. This gives
$6\cdot14/2=42$ elements; they are the elements $\gamma_{q,a}f^3$ identified in the
proof of Proposition~\ref{per:prop:fixed}, so they lie in $f^3\Gamma$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{wh:lem:model}
Let $\psi:\Lambda\to\mathbb Z/6\subset\mathbb R/6\mathbb Z$ be the homomorphism with kernel
$\Gamma$ and $\psi(f)=-1$. Then
\[
 M_7\cong_{\mathrm{diff}}(S^3\times\mathbb R/6\mathbb Z)\big/\Lambda,\;\;\;
 \lambda\cdot(v,s)=(\lambda v,\,s+\psi(\lambda)),
\]
and the action is free. The canonical action of
Theorem~\ref{per:thm:action} is translation of the second factor, and its
orbit map is the projection to $S^3/\Lambda=X$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
In \eqref{per:eq:torus}, the map $T:=\gamma_{-1,0}D^6$ is $(v,s)\mapsto(v,s+6)$,
because $f^{-6}=-\mathrm{id}$, and it is central. An element of $G_7$ with base
degree $k$ acts on $S^3$ by an element of $f^{-k}\Gamma$. Such an element is
trivial on $S^3$ only when $6\mid k$, so the kernel of $G_7\to\operatorname{Isom}(S^3)$ is
$\langle T\rangle$.
Indeed, for $k=6l$ the element $\gamma_{q,a}D^{6l}$ acts by
$\gamma_{q,a}f^{-6l}=\gamma_{q,a}\gamma_{(-1)^l,0}$, which is trivial only
when $(q,a)=((-1)^l,0)$; the element is then $(\gamma_{-1,0}D^6)^l=T^l$. The image of this map is $\Lambda$, and the translation
part modulo $6$ is the homomorphism $\psi$. Hence
$M_7=\bigl((S^3\times\mathbb R)/\langle T\rangle\bigr)\big/(G_7/\langle T\rangle)$
is the displayed quotient. Freeness follows from
Proposition~\ref{wh:prop:product}(iv): an element with a fixed point on $S^3$
is an involution in $f^3\Gamma$, and it translates the circle factor by
$3\ne0$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{wh:lem:underlying}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item The nontrivial elements of $\Lambda$ with a fixed point on $S^3$
      are exactly the $42$ involutions $\gamma_{q,a}f^3$ with
      $q\in\{\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ and $a\in\mathbb Z/7$. The subgroup they
      generate is $\Lambda_0=\langle\Gamma,f^3\rangle=Q_8\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}}Q_{28}$, of order
      $112$; it is normal, and $\Lambda/\Lambda_0\cong C_3$ is generated by
      the image of $f$.
\item $\pi_1(|X|)\cong C_3$, and $|X|$ is a closed orientable
      three-manifold homeomorphic, hence diffeomorphic, to $L(3,1)$.
\item $|S^3/\Lambda_0|$ is homeomorphic to $S^3$, and $|X|$ is its
      quotient by a free action of $C_3=\Lambda/\Lambda_0$.
\item The singular circle $\mathcal S$ is a tame knot in $|X|$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
(i) Every element of $\Lambda$ has the form $\gamma_{q,a}f^n$ with
$0\le n\le5$, since $f^6=\gamma_{-1,0}$ by
Theorem~\ref{per:thm:periodic}(i). For $n=0$ only the identity has a fixed
point, because $\Gamma$ acts freely; for $n\in\{1,2,4,5\}$ no element
has one, because $\operatorname{Fix}(\bar f^{\,n})=\emptyset$ on $N_7$
(Proposition~\ref{per:prop:fixed}); for $n=3$ the fixed-point criterion
of Lemma~\ref{per:lem:rigidity} gives exactly $q\in\{\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$,
as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{per:prop:fixed}. These elements have
order two by Proposition~\ref{wh:prop:product}(iv), where $(A,B)^2=(-1,-1)$ is
computed directly. For any two of these involutions,
\[
 (\gamma_{q,a}f^3)(\gamma_{q',a'}f^3)^{-1}
 =\gamma_{q,a}\gamma_{q',a'}^{-1}=\gamma_{qq'^{-1},\,a-a'}.
\]
Taking $q=q'$ gives $C_7$, and taking $(q,q')=(i,j)$, $(j,k)$ and $(k,i)$ gives
$-k$, $-i$ and $-j$, which generate $Q_8$; hence the subgroup generated by the
involutions contains $\Gamma$ and also $f^3=\gamma_{i,0}^{-1}(\gamma_{i,0}f^3)$. Conversely, every
$\gamma_{q,a}f^3$ lies in $\langle\Gamma,f^3\rangle$. This subgroup is
normal, since $f$ normalizes $\Gamma$ and commutes with $f^3$, and it
has order $2\cdot56$ because $f^3\notin\Gamma$ and $f^6\in\Gamma$
(Theorem~\ref{per:thm:periodic}(ii)). The quotient has order three and is
generated by $f$. In the notation of Proposition~\ref{wh:prop:product},
$f^3=(1,-j)$, so $\Lambda_0=Q_8\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}}\langle C_{14},j\rangle=Q_8\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}}Q_{28}$.

(ii) Armstrong's theorem \cite{Armstrong1968} identifies $\pi_1(|X|)$
with the quotient of $\Lambda$ by the normal subgroup generated by the
elements having fixed points. By (i), this quotient is
$\Lambda/\Lambda_0\cong C_3$.
Locally, $|X|$ is a quotient of a ball by a rotation group of order at
most two, and $D^3/C_2\cong D^3$; hence $|X|$ is a closed topological
three-manifold. It is orientable because $\Lambda$ acts on $S^3$ by
two-sided unit-quaternion multiplications, which preserve orientation.
By the results of Moise and Munkres \cite{Moise1977,Munkres1960}, it has a smooth
structure, unique up to diffeomorphism. By elliptization \cite{PerelmanEntropy,PerelmanSurg,PerelmanExt}, a
closed three-manifold with
fundamental group $C_3$ is a spherical space form with cyclic fundamental
group of order three, that is, $L(3,1)$ or $L(3,2)$ \cite[Part~III]{Wolf2011}; these are diffeomorphic as
unoriented manifolds.

(iii) The same argument applied to $\Lambda_0$, whose elements with fixed
points are the same $42$ involutions and generate $\Lambda_0$ by (i),
shows that $|S^3/\Lambda_0|$ is a simply connected closed three-manifold,
hence $S^3$ by the three-dimensional Poincar\'e conjecture
\cite{PerelmanEntropy,PerelmanSurg,PerelmanExt}. If $g\in\Lambda\setminus\Lambda_0$ carried a
$\Lambda_0$-orbit to itself, say $g v=hv$ with $h\in\Lambda_0$, then
$h^{-1}g\in\Lambda\setminus\Lambda_0$ would have a fixed point, contrary
to (i). So $\Lambda/\Lambda_0$ acts freely.

(iv) In an orbifold chart $D^3/C_2$, the singular set is the image of the
rotation axis, which the homeomorphism
$(re^{i\theta},x)\mapsto(re^{2i\theta},x)$ onto $D^3$ carries to a
straight segment.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{wh:thm:branched}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $N':=S^3/\Lambda^+$ is a spherical space form with
      $\pi_1N'\congT^{*}\times C_7$ and $H_1(N')\cong\mathbb Z/21$. The deck
      involution $\iota$ of $N'\to X$ has a connected fixed set, which maps
      homeomorphically onto $\mathcal S$. Hence, $N'$ is the double cover of
      $|X|\congL(3,1)$ branched along $\mathcal S$.
\item Let $\widetilde X=|S^3/\Lambda_0|$. This is $S^3$, and it is the
      universal cover of $|X|$ (Lemma~\ref{wh:lem:underlying}). The preimage
      of $\mathcal S$ in this cover is a three-component link $L_0$, whose components
      are permuted cyclically by the deck group $C_3=\Lambda/\Lambda_0$. The
      manifold $N_7=S^3/\Gamma$ is the double cover of $S^3$ branched along
      $L_0$, with covering involution $\bar f^{\,3}$.
\item $\mathcal S$ is null-homotopic in $|X|$, and
      $H_1(E_{\mathcal S})\cong\mathbb Z\langle\mu\rangle\oplus\mathbb Z/3$. Here $\mu$ is
      a meridian, and the torsion summand maps isomorphically to
      $H_1(|X|)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
(i) The group $\Lambda^+$ acts freely by
Proposition~\ref{wh:prop:product}(iii). The abelianization of
$T^{*}\times C_7$ is $C_3\times C_7$. We have $X=N'/(\Lambda/\Lambda^+)$, and
the nontrivial element acts by an involution $\iota$. The fixed set of
$\iota$ is the image of the fixed circles of the $42$ involutions. These
circles are pairwise disjoint: a common point would be fixed by a nontrivial
element of $\Lambda^+$. The $42$ involutions form one $\Lambda^+$-conjugacy class. Put $\xi:=-\zeta$;
this is a generator of $C_{14}$, of order $14$, with $\xi^7=-1$, and
$Q_{28}\setminus C_{14}=\{\xi^mj:m\in\mathbb Z/14\}$. With the conventions of
Proposition~\ref{wh:prop:product}, the involutions are the elements
$(A,\xi^mj)$ with $A\in\{i,j,k\}$ and $m\in\mathbb Z/14$, since $(-A,B)=(A,-B)$ and
$-\xi^mj=\xi^{m+7}j$. Conjugation by $(\omega,1)$ permutes $i$, $j$ and $k$
cyclically; conjugation by $(1,\zeta)$ sends $(A,\xi^mj)$ to
$(A,\zeta^{-1}\xi^mj\zeta)=(A,\xi^{m-2}j)$, because $j\zeta=\zeta^{-1}j$ and
$\zeta^{-2}=\xi^{-2}$; and conjugation by $(j,1)$ sends $(i,\xi^mj)$ to
$(-i,\xi^mj)=(i,\xi^{m+7}j)$. The translations $m\mapsto m-2$ and
$m\mapsto m+7$ generate all translations of $\mathbb Z/14$. Hence, the fixed circles form one $\Lambda^+$-orbit, so $\operatorname{Fix}(\iota)$ is
the image in $N'$ of a single fixed circle $\operatorname{Fix}(g)$, where $g$ is one of
the $42$ involutions. If $h\in\Lambda^+$ satisfies $h\operatorname{Fix}(g)=\operatorname{Fix}(g)$,
then $hgh^{-1}$ fixes $\operatorname{Fix}(g)$ pointwise. Since the fixed circles are
pairwise disjoint, the only elements of $\Lambda$ fixing a point of
