$\operatorname{Fix}(g)$ are $1$ and $g$; hence $hgh^{-1}=g$. Thus, the stabilizer of
$\operatorname{Fix}(g)$ in $\Lambda^+$ is the centralizer of $g$ in $\Lambda^+$, of
order $168/42=4$, and it acts freely on the circle $\operatorname{Fix}(g)$ because
$\Lambda^+$ acts freely on $S^3$. The quotient of a circle by a free
action of a finite group is a circle, so $\operatorname{Fix}(\iota)$ is an embedded
circle in $N'$, and the restriction of the quotient map $N'\to X$ to $\operatorname{Fix}(\iota)$
maps this circle bijectively onto the branch locus $\mathcal S$.

(ii) The components of the preimage of $\mathcal S$ in $\widetilde X$ are the
images of the $42$ circles modulo $\Lambda_0$. These correspond to the
$\Lambda_0$-conjugacy classes of the involutions. An element $(C,D)$ of
$\Lambda_0=Q_8\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}}Q_{28}$ has $C\in Q_8$, and conjugation by $C$ preserves each
of the sets $\{\pm i\}$, $\{\pm j\}$ and $\{\pm k\}$; so the left axis of an
involution is a conjugacy-class invariant, and there are at least three classes. By the
computation in (i), applied with $(1,\zeta)$, with $(p,1)$ for an element
$p\in Q_8$ anticommuting with the left axis (so that
$(A,\xi^mj)\mapsto(A,-\xi^mj)=(A,\xi^{m+7}j)$), and with $(1,j)$ (which
sends $(A,\xi^mj)$ to $(A,\xi^{-m}j)$), the
$14$ involutions with a given left axis are conjugate in $\Lambda_0$. So
there are exactly three classes, of $14$ elements each, and $L_0$ has three
components. Each component is an embedded circle. Indeed, let $g$ be one of the
involutions. If $h\in\Lambda_0$ preserves $\operatorname{Fix}(g)$, then $hgh^{-1}$ fixes
$\operatorname{Fix}(g)$ pointwise, so $hgh^{-1}=g$ as in~(i). By
Lemma~\ref{wh:lem:underlying}(i) and the disjointness of the $42$ fixed
circles, the only elements of $\Lambda_0$ fixing a point of $\operatorname{Fix}(g)$ are $1$
and $g$. Hence $\operatorname{Stab}_{\Lambda_0}(\operatorname{Fix}(g))/\langle g\rangle$ acts freely on the
circle $\operatorname{Fix}(g)$, and the image of $\operatorname{Fix}(g)$ in $\widetilde X$ is an embedded
circle, tame by the chart argument of Lemma~\ref{wh:lem:underlying}(iv).
The element $f=(\omega^{-1},j)$ conjugates the left axes
cyclically, so it permutes the three components cyclically; compare the
proof of Proposition~\ref{per:prop:fixed}. Finally, $\Lambda_0/\Gamma$ is
generated by $f^3$. This proves the statement about $N_7$.

(iii) By (ii), the universal covering
$\widetilde X\to |X|$ has degree three and the full preimage of
$\mathcal S$ has exactly three components. Hence, each of those components
maps with degree one onto $\mathcal S$. Equivalently, a loop running once
along $\mathcal S$ has a closed lift to the universal cover, so the element of
$\pi_1(|X|)$ that it represents is trivial. Thus, $\mathcal S$ is null-homotopic. For a null-homologous knot in a rational homology
sphere, the Mayer--Vietoris sequence gives
$H_1(E_{\mathcal S})\cong\mathbb Z\langle\mu\rangle\oplus H_1(|X|)$, where the projection
to $\mathbb Z\langle\mu\rangle$ is given by intersection with a Seifert surface for
$\mathcal S$; compare \cite[Section~2.3]{GordonLidman2014}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{wh:rem:seifert}
In the stabilizer calculations below, we fix a Hopf circle in $S^3$ and
take its setwise stabilizer in the specified finite group. The isotropy
group at each point of $X$ is trivial or cyclic of order two.

The group
$\Lambda=T^{*}\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}}Q_{28}$ preserves the Hopf fibration $v\mapsto vU(1)$ of
$S^3$, because $Q_{28}\subset U(1)\cup U(1)j$ normalizes $U(1)$. Under the Hopf
map $h(v)=vi\bar v$, an element $(A,B)$ acts on the base $S^2$ by
$x\mapsto AxA^{-1}$ if $B\in C_{14}$ and by $x\mapsto-AxA^{-1}$ if
$B\inQ_{28}\setminus C_{14}$. The induced group is the pyritohedral group
$A_4\times\{\pm1\}$ of order $24$, and the kernel is
$C_{14}=\{(1,B):B\in C_{14}\}$. Hence, $X$ is a Seifert-fibred orbifold over
the two-orbifold $S^2/(A_4\times\{\pm1\})$, a disc with one cone point of
order three and a mirror boundary carrying one corner reflector of order two
(the orbifold $3{*}2$ in Conway's notation \cite{Conway1992}). The $42$
involutions act on
the base by reflections, so $\mathcal S$ lies over the mirror boundary:
over a mirror point the fibre of $X$ is an interval whose two endpoints lie
on $\mathcal S$. The fibre over the cone point of order three has stabilizer
$\langle-\omega\rangle\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}} C_{14}\cong C_{42}$, which acts freely on it, so
this fibre is exceptional, with multiplicity $42/14=3$. Traversing this
exceptional fibre once represents a generator of its stabilizer, an element
of order $42$ in $\Lambda=\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(X)$; the cube of this element generates the
kernel $C_{14}$, that is, it is the class of a regular fibre up to
orientation. The fibre over
the corner reflector has stabilizer $\langle(i,\zeta),(j,j)\rangle$, which is dihedral
of order $56$, since $(j,j)$ inverts $(i,\zeta)$. The same computation for
$\Lambda_0=Q_8\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}}Q_{28}$ gives a Seifert structure on $S^3/\Lambda_0$ over the
orbifold ${*}222$, a disc with three corner reflectors of order two, with
one singular circle over each of the three mirror edges; these circles form the
three-component link $L_0$ of Theorem~\ref{wh:thm:branched}(ii). The same invariants follow from the closed formulas in
\cite{MecchiaSeppi2015} and are tabulated in \cite{MecchiaSchilling2025}:
in \cite[Table~5]{MecchiaSchilling2025} the quotient of the
tetrahedral manifold $N'$ by the involution with extension $\Lambda$
(Family~14, $m=7$) is listed with base orbifold $D^2(3;2)$, local
invariants $7/2$ and $7/3$, and Euler class $-7/12$; in
\cite[Table~7]{MecchiaSchilling2025} the quotient of the prism manifold
$N_7$ by the
involution with extension $\Lambda_0$ (Family~10, $m=7$) is listed with
base orbifold $D^2(;2,2,2)$, local invariants $7/2$, $7/2$ and $7/2$, and Euler
class $-7/4$, up to the orientation convention.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{wh:rem:tables}
The orbifold $S^3/\Lambda_0$ fibres over $D^2(;2,2,2)$, a disc without cone
points. Its underlying space is therefore $S^3$ by
\cite[Proposition~2.10]{Dunbar1981}; see also
\cite[Section~5.3]{MecchiaSchilling2025}. The orbifold $X$ fibres over
$D^2(3;2)$, whose cone point has the nonintegral local invariant $7/3$.
Thus, $|X|\not\cong S^3$ by \cite[Proposition~2.11]{Dunbar1981}.
The involution $\bar f^{\,3}$ of $N_7$, with extension $\Lambda_0$
(Family~10), is hyperelliptic, whereas the involution $\iota$ of $N'$, with
extension $\Lambda$ (Family~14), is not
\cite[Tables~11 and~13]{MecchiaSchilling2025}.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{wh:lem:abel}
For either mirror image of the Whitehead link,
$H_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal O_{W})=\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal O_{W})^{\mathrm{ab}}$ is cyclic of
order six. The images of a meridian $\mu_J$ of $J$ and of a meridian
$\mu_{W'}$ of $W'$ have orders three and two, and their product is a
generator.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The orbifold group is $\pi_1(S^3\setminus(J\cup W'))$ modulo the normal
closure of the surgery slope $\mu_J^3\lambda_J$ and of $\mu_{W'}^{\,2}$.
By Alexander duality \cite[Theorem~3.44]{Hatcher},
$H_1(S^3\setminus(J\cup W'))=\mathbb Z\mu_J\oplus\mathbb Z\mu_{W'}$,
and the Seifert longitude of $J$ represents $\lambda_J=\operatorname{lk}(J,W')\,\mu_{W'}=0$ in this group.
Hence
$H_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal O_{W})=\mathbb Z^2/\langle3\mu_J,2\mu_{W'}\rangle\cong\mathbb Z/3\oplus\mathbb Z/2$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{wh:prop:lift}
Let $W=J\cup W'$ be either mirror image of the Whitehead link, and let $Y$ be
the double cover of $S^3_{+3}(J)$ branched along $W'$. Let
$w\in\{2,-2\}$ be the writhe of the standard clasp diagram of $J$ in the
solid torus $V=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu W'$, that is, the sum of the signs of its
two self-crossings (the signs are equal, as they are at every clasp), and put $m=-w$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item The double cover of $S^3$ branched along $W'$ is $S^3$, and the
      preimage $\widetilde J=\widetilde J_1\cup\widetilde J_2$ of $J$ in this cover is
      the torus link $T(2,2m)$: its components are unknotted and cobound an
      annulus with an unknotted core and framing $m$.
\item The surgery slope $3\mu_J+\lambda_J$ lifts on each $\widetilde J_i$ to
      the slope $(3+m)\widetilde\mu_i+\widetilde\lambda_i^{\,0}$, where
      $\widetilde\lambda_i^{\,0}$ is the Seifert longitude of $\widetilde J_i$.
      Hence, $Y=S^3_{3+m,\,3+m}\bigl(T(2,2m)\bigr)$ and
      $|H_1(Y)|=|(3+m)^2-m^2|=|9+6m|$.
\item $Y$ is Seifert fibred over $S^2(2,3,3)$: the components of $T(2,2m)$
      are regular fibres of the Seifert fibration of $S^3$ by
      $(1,m)$-torus curves, whose fibre framing is $m$, and the lifted slopes
      are $3\widetilde\mu_i+\lambda_{\mathrm{fib}}$.
\item For $m=2$ one has $|H_1(Y)|=21$, and for $m=-2$ one has $|H_1(Y)|=3$.
      Thus, the two mirror images are distinguished by $|H_1(Y)|$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
(i) Since $W'$ is unknotted, we have $\Sigma_2(S^3,W')=S^3$. Since
$\operatorname{lk}(J,W')=0$, the preimage of $J$ has two components,
$\widetilde J_1$ and $\widetilde J_2$, interchanged by the deck involution. Let
$\widetilde\lambda_i$ be the lift of the Seifert longitude $\lambda_J$ to
$\partial\nu\widetilde J_i$. For $w=2$, the calculation in \cite[Section~5]{GordonLidman2014}
shows, with the two components interchanged by the symmetry of the Whitehead
link, that $\widetilde J$ is the torus link $T(2,-4)$ (denoted $T_{-2,4}$
there) and that the blackboard longitude $\lambda_J+w\mu_J$ lifts to the
Seifert longitudes of the $\widetilde J_i$. Hence
$\operatorname{lk}(\widetilde J_i,\widetilde\lambda_i)=-w=m$, and $\widetilde J$ is the
boundary of an annulus with an unknotted core and framing $m$, that is,
$T(2,2m)$. The case $w=-2$ follows by applying an orientation-reversing
diffeomorphism of $S^3$, which changes the signs of $w$, of $m$ and of all
linking numbers.

\emph{A self-contained check of~(i).} The identification of $\widetilde J$
can also be read off from the diagram. Project the clasp diagram of $J$ in the
annulus along the axis $W'$. The double cover branched along $W'$ is
$\vartheta\mapsto2\vartheta$ in cylindrical coordinates, so it commutes with
this projection: the lifted diagram consists of two copies of the band of $J$,
each running half way around, and two copies of the clasp, each now between
$\widetilde J_1$ and $\widetilde J_2$ and with the same crossing signs. Hence
each $\widetilde J_i$ has a crossingless diagram, so it is unknotted and its
blackboard framing is its Seifert framing; since the blackboard longitude
$\lambda_J+w\mu_J$ lifts to the blackboard longitudes,
$\widetilde\lambda_i=\widetilde\lambda_i^{\,0}-w\widetilde\mu_i$. With the
lifted orientations the four mixed crossings have signs summing to $2w$, so
$\operatorname{lk}(\widetilde J_1,\widetilde J_2)=w$. Seifert's algorithm applied to the
clasp diagram of $J$ gives three Seifert circles and two bands, hence a disc
$\Delta$ with $\partial\Delta=J$; exactly two of the circles encircle the
axis, so $\Delta$ meets $W'$ transversely in two points. Its preimage
$\widetilde\Delta$, the double cover of a disc branched at two points, is an
annulus with $\partial\widetilde\Delta=\widetilde J_1\sqcup\widetilde J_2$, and
the lifted orientations are its boundary orientation. Its core is isotopic to
$\widetilde J_1$, hence unknotted. For the boundary orientation of an annulus
with $k$ full twists the two boundary circles have linking number $-k$, so
$k=-w=m$ and $\widetilde J=T(2,2m)$, for either sign of $w$.

(ii) The lift of $\mu_J$ is the meridian $\widetilde\mu_i$ of $\widetilde J_i$,
and the lift of $\lambda_J$ is $\widetilde\lambda_i$, with
$\operatorname{lk}(\widetilde J_i,\widetilde\lambda_i)=m$ by (i), so
$\widetilde\lambda_i=\widetilde\lambda_i^{\,0}+m\widetilde\mu_i$ and the
lifted slope is $(3+m)\widetilde\mu_i+\widetilde\lambda_i^{\,0}$. The double
cover of $S^3_{+3}(J)$ branched along $W'$ is obtained from
$\Sigma_2(S^3,W')=S^3$ by surgery along $\widetilde J$ with the lifted
slopes, because the surgery solid torus is disjoint from $W'$ and its boundary
torus lifts to two tori. With parallel orientations, the components of
$T(2,2m)$ have linking number $m$, so the linking matrix of the surgery is
$\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}3+m&m\\m&3+m\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, and
its determinant is $(3+m)^2-m^2$.

(iii) Two parallel $(1,m)$-torus curves on the standard torus form
$T(2,2m)$ and have linking number $m$. They are regular fibres of the Seifert
fibration of $S^3$ whose fibres are the $(1,m)$-curves; it has one exceptional
fibre, of multiplicity $|m|=2$, and the fibre framing of a regular fibre is
$m$ (the framing of a $(p,q)$-torus knot induced by a neighbouring fibre is
$pq$ \cite{Moser1971}), so
$\lambda_{\mathrm{fib}}=\widetilde\lambda_i^{\,0}+m\widetilde\mu_i$
and the lifted slope is $3\widetilde\mu_i+\lambda_{\mathrm{fib}}$. It meets
the fibre slope three times, so each of the two surgeries replaces a regular
fibre by an exceptional fibre of multiplicity three, and $Y$ is Seifert
fibred over $S^2(2,3,3)$.

(iv) Substitute $m=\pm2$ in (ii).
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{wh:thm:whitehead}
For the mirror image of the Whitehead link fixed above, there is a
homeomorphism of orbifolds $X\cong\mathcal O_{W}$, possibly reversing orientation. In
particular,
\[
 (|X|,\mathcal S)\ \cong\ \bigl(S^3_{+3}(J),\,W'\bigr).
\]
Under this homeomorphism, the singular circle is the Whitehead partner of a $(+3)$-surgery curve.
Equivalently, $\mathcal S$ lies in one solid torus of a genus-one Heegaard
splitting of $L(3,1)$ as a Whitehead double of its core, with the twisting
of the Whitehead link.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
By the mirror convention, $m=2$ in Proposition~\ref{wh:prop:lift};
equivalently, the double cover of $S^3_{+3}(J)$ branched along $W'$ has
first homology of order $21$. Let $Y$ be this double cover of
$S^3_{+3}(J)$ branched along $W'$. It exists because $W'$ is null-homologous:
$\operatorname{lk}(J,W')=0$. By Proposition~\ref{wh:prop:lift}, $Y$ is Seifert fibred over
$S^2(2,3,3)$ with $|H_1(Y)|=21$. In the notation of normalized Seifert invariants \cite{Orlik1972},
$Y=M(0;b;(2,1),(3,\beta_2),(3,\beta_3))$ with $\beta_i\in\{1,2\}$, and
$|H_1(Y)|=|18b+9+6(\beta_2+\beta_3)|=21$. The only solutions are $b=0$ with
$\beta_2=\beta_3=1$, and $b=-3$ with $\beta_2=\beta_3=2$, which are the two
orientations of one manifold. Indeed, reversing the orientation sends the normalized invariants
$M\bigl(0;b;(\alpha_1,\beta_1),\ldots,(\alpha_n,\beta_n)\bigr)$ to
$M\bigl(0;-n-b;(\alpha_1,\alpha_1-\beta_1),\ldots,(\alpha_n,\alpha_n-\beta_n)\bigr)$
\cite{Orlik1972}, \cite[Section~2.4, formula~(2.1)]{GordonLidman2014}; here
$n=3$.

The Hopf fibration $v\mapsto vi\bar v$ descends to $N'=S^3/\Lambda^+$:
its base action is the tetrahedral rotation group $A_4$, so the base is
$S^2(2,3,3)$; compare Remark~\ref{wh:rem:seifert} and \cite{Scott1983}.
Since $|H_1(N')|=21$ by Theorem~\ref{wh:thm:branched}(i), the same calculation
with normalized Seifert invariants identifies $Y$ with $N'$ up to orientation.
The homeomorphism may be replaced by a diffeomorphism
\cite{Moise1977,Munkres1960}.

Transport the covering involution of $Y$ to $N'$ by this diffeomorphism.
It is orientation-preserving even if the chosen diffeomorphism reverses
orientation. By \cite[Theorem~E and Section~2.1]{DinkelbachLeeb}, the
transported action is smoothly conjugate to an isometric action for the
standard spherical quotient metric on $N'$. Here the use of the fixed
quotient metric is justified by the uniqueness of an elliptic geometric
structure up to diffeomorphism, as recalled in Section~2.1 of that paper;
compare the classical spherical-space-form classification
\cite{ThrelfallSeifert1931,ThrelfallSeifert1933,Wolf2011} and
\cite[Section~8]{deRham1950}. An isometry of $N'$ lifts through its universal
Riemannian covering to an isometry of $S^3$ normalizing $\Lambda^+$.
Thus the covering involution has an orientation-preserving lift $(C,D)$,
and the full lifted group contains $\Lambda^+$ with index two. Therefore
$\mathcal O_{W}\cong S^3/\Lambda_W$, where
$\Lambda_W=\langle\Lambda^+,(C,D)\rangle\subset SO(4)$ contains $\Lambda^+$ as a subgroup of index two and normalizes it. We also have
$\Lambda_W\cong\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal O_{W})$, so
$\Lambda_W^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong C_6$ by Lemma~\ref{wh:lem:abel}. No element of $O(4)\setminus SO(4)$
normalizes $\Lambda^+$, because an orientation-reversing isometry of $S^3$
interchanges the left and right factors, whereas the two projections of
$\Lambda^+$ are the nonisomorphic groups $T^{*}$ and $C_{14}$. The
standard normalizers of binary polyhedral and cyclic subgroups of the unit
quaternions \cite{DuVal1964,ConwaySmith2003} show that normalizing $\Lambda^+$
requires
\[
   C\in N_{S^3}(T^{*})=O^*,\;\;\;
   D\in N_{S^3}(C_{14})=U(1)\cup U(1)j.
\]

\emph{Step 1: $C\inT^{*}$.} Suppose instead that $C\in O^*\setminusT^{*}$. Then
conjugation by $(C,D)$ restricts to the nontrivial outer automorphism of
$T^{*}$ and inverts $T^{*}/Q_8\cong C_3$. In
$\Lambda_W^{\mathrm{ab}}$ the image $x$ of $(\omega,1)$ therefore satisfies
$x=x^{-1}$ and $x^3=1$, so $x=1$. The image of
$Q_8\times1\subseteq[\Lambda^+,\Lambda^+]$ is also trivial; hence the entire
left factor $T^{*}\times1$ has trivial image in the abelianization.

Now $O^*/Q_8\cong S_3$ and $T^{*}/Q_8\cong A_3$. Thus
$C\notinT^{*}$ implies $C^2\in Q_8$. Since $(C,D)$ represents the nontrivial
coset of the index-two extension $\Lambda_W/\Lambda^+$, we also have
$(C,D)^2\in\Lambda^+$, and consequently $D^2\in C_{14}$. If $y$ denotes the
image of $(C,D)$ in $\Lambda_W^{\mathrm{ab}}$, this abelianization is therefore
generated by the image of $C_{14}$ and by $y$, with $y^2$ lying in the image
of $C_{14}$. The image of $C_{14}$ has order dividing $14$, so this
abelianization has no $3$-torsion. This contradicts
$\Lambda_W^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong C_6$. Hence, $C\inT^{*}$, and by replacing $(C,D)$
with $(C^{-1},1)(C,D)$, we may take $C=1$.

\emph{Step 2: $D\notin U(1)$.} Suppose that $D\in U(1)$. Then the finite cyclic
group $\langle C_{14},D\rangle\subset U(1)$ contains $C_{14}$ with index two,
so it is $C_{28}$ and $\Lambda_W=T^{*}\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}} C_{28}$. Since
$[T^{*},T^{*}]=Q_8$ contains $-1$, abelianization kills the diagonal relation
$(-1,-1)$ on the left and therefore also kills the order-two element of
$C_{28}$. Hence
\[
  \Lambda_W^{\mathrm{ab}}
     \cong (T^{*})^{\mathrm{ab}}\times
            \bigl(C_{28}/\langle-1\rangle\bigr)
     \cong C_3\times C_{14},
\]
which has order $42$, contradicting
$\Lambda_W^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong C_6$. Thus, $D\in U(1)j$, and
$R=\langle C_{14},D\rangle$ is binary dihedral of order $28$.

\emph{Step 3: conjugation to $\Lambda$.} Conjugation by $(1,u)$ with
$u\in U(1)$ fixes $\Lambda^+$ elementwise and sends $e^{i\varphi}j$ to
$e^{i\varphi}u^{-2}j$. Choosing $u^2=e^{i\varphi}$ gives $D=j$, so $\Lambda_W$
is conjugate to $T^{*}\mathbin{\times_{\pm1}}Q_{28}=\Lambda$. Hence
$\mathcal O_{W}\cong S^3/\Lambda=X$.

For the other mirror image, the corresponding double cover has first homology of
order $3$ (Proposition~\ref{wh:prop:lift}(iv)), so it is not homeomorphic
to $N'$, and the corresponding orbifold is not homeomorphic to $X$: an
orbifold homeomorphism would carry the orbifold cover $N'\to X$ to the
double cover branched along $W'$, since $\Lambda^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong C_6$
has exactly one subgroup of index two and both covers correspond to it.

For the Heegaard description, note that $J$ is unknotted, so the complement of
$\nu J$ in $S^3$ is a solid torus. Its core is a meridian circle of $J$, and
$W'$ is the Whitehead double of that core inside it, untwisted with respect
to the framing induced from $S^3$. The surgery solid torus is the other
Heegaard solid torus.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{wh:thm:section}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item For every admissible $\ell$, the unit section $\gamma_\ell$ is a
      weight circle. Hence, by Lemma~\ref{lem:weight-loops}, its framed
      surgeries are represented by \eqref{eq:candidates}, up to the
      orientation of the belt sphere.
\item In the Whitehead model of Theorem~\ref{wh:thm:whitehead}, let $\ell$
      be any band sum, in $E_{\mathcal S}$, of a meridian $\mu_J$ of the
      surgery curve and a meridian $\mu_{W'}$ of $\mathcal S=W'$. Then
      $\ell$ is admissible and $\operatorname{lk}(\ell,\mathcal S)=\pm1$.
\item In particular, $\Sigma_+(7)$ and $\Sigma_-(7)$ are the two framed
      surgeries on $\gamma_\ell$ for such an $\ell$, with the two
      framings identified only as an unordered pair.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
(i) By construction $\gamma_\ell$ is embedded and has degree one under
$p_*$. Lemma~\ref{lem:weight-loops} shows that every such element normally
generates $G_7$, so $\gamma_\ell$ is a weight circle in the group-theoretic
sense. The same lemma identifies the unordered pair of framed-surgery
outputs.

(ii) The homeomorphism of Theorem~\ref{wh:thm:whitehead} induces an
isomorphism $\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal O_{W})\cong\Lambda$, hence an isomorphism of
abelianizations $H_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal O_{W})\cong\Lambda^{\mathrm{ab}}=C_6$. By
Lemma~\ref{wh:lem:abel}, the image of $\mu_J$ has order three and the image
of $\mu_{W'}$ has order two. (The latter is also visible in $\Lambda$: the
meridian $\mu_{W'}$ maps to one of the $42$ involutions, whose left part
lies in $Q_8$ and whose right part lies in $Q_{28}\setminus C_{14}$.)
A band sum represents a based product
$\mu_J\cdot g\mu_{W'}^{\pm1}g^{-1}$. Its image is the product of these two
images, which generates $C_6$. For the linking number,
$\operatorname{lk}(\mu_J,W')=0$ and $\operatorname{lk}(\mu_{W'},W')=\pm1$. Here $\operatorname{lk}(\cdot,\mathcal S)$ is the intersection number with a Seifert
surface for the null-homologous knot $\mathcal S$ in the rational homology
sphere $|X|$ (Theorem~\ref{wh:thm:branched}(iii)); it depends only on the
class in $H_1(E_{\mathcal S})$ and is therefore additive under band sums.
Since $\operatorname{lk}(J,W')=0$ in $S^3$, the knot $W'$ bounds a Seifert surface in
$S^3\setminus\nu J\subset|X|$. This surface is disjoint from a meridian $\mu_J$
chosen on $\partial\nu J$; this gives $\operatorname{lk}(\mu_J,W')=0$.

(iii) Combine (i) and (ii). The unordered pair is the pair described in
Lemma~\ref{lem:weight-loops} and Theorem~\ref{thm:rigidity}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{wh:cor:input}
Let $\chi$ be either of the two surjections
$\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal O_{W})\to C_6\subset S^1$. Then $\chi(\mu_J)$ has order
three and $\chi(\mu_{W'})$ has order two. Up to orientation,
\[
 M_7\cong_{\mathrm{diff}} M(\mathcal O_{W},\chi).
\]
For every band sum $\ell=\mu_J\natural\mu_{W'}$, the manifolds
$\Sigma_\pm(7)$ are the two framed surgeries on the unit section
$\gamma_\ell$. Consequently, the framed-surgery pair is determined by a
single two-component link diagram: the Whitehead link, with coefficient
$+3$ on $J$ and cone angle $\pi$ on $W'$, together with a band and a choice of
framing parity.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{wh:lem:model} gives $M_7\cong_{\mathrm{diff}} M(X,\psi)$.
The space $M(\mathcal O_{W},\chi)$ is defined: by Theorem~\ref{wh:thm:whitehead} the
universal orbifold cover of $\mathcal O_{W}$ is $S^3$, and every isotropy subgroup of
$\mathcal O_{W}$ is conjugate to $\langle\mu_{W'}\rangle$, on which $\chi$ is injective
because $\chi(\mu_{W'})$ has order two. The orbifold
homeomorphism $\mathcal O_{W}\cong X$ of Theorem~\ref{wh:thm:whitehead} is covered by
a diffeomorphism $\Phi:S^3\to S^3$ of the universal covers that is
equivariant with respect to an isomorphism
$\varphi:\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal O_{W})\to\Lambda$: the smooth conjugacy of the
covering involution of $Y\cong N'$ to an isometry lifts to the universal
covers equivariantly with respect to the lifted groups, and the remaining
identifications in that proof are isometries of $S^3$. For a character
$\chi=\psi\circ\varphi$, the map $(x,u)\mapsto(\Phi(x),u)$ descends to a
diffeomorphism $M(\mathcal O_{W},\chi)\to M(X,\psi)$ whose effect on orientation is the same as that of $\Phi$. The group $\Lambda^{\mathrm{ab}}$
is $C_6$, and its only automorphisms are $\pm1$. So the induced character is
$\chi^{\pm1}$, and replacing $\chi$ by $\chi^{-1}$ reverses the circle. The
orders of $\chi(\mu_J)$ and $\chi(\mu_{W'})$ were computed in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{wh:thm:section}(ii). The remaining statement follows from
Theorem~\ref{wh:thm:section}(iii).
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{std:thm:main}
\[
 \Sigma_+(7)\cong_{\mathrm{diff}} S^4\;\;\;\text{and}\;\;\;\Sigma_-(7)\cong_{\mathrm{diff}} S^4.
\]
In particular, neither resulting manifold is an exotic four-sphere.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{std:def:data}
Let $Y$ be a closed connected oriented smooth four-manifold with a smooth
effective circle action without fixed points, and let $\pi:Y\to Q=Y/S^1$ be
the orbit map onto the closed orientable three-orbifold $Q$. Let $\ell\subset
Q$ be a smoothly embedded loop in the free stratum, let
$T_\ell=\pi^{-1}(\ell)$, and let $\gamma\subset T_\ell$ be a section of the
circle bundle $T_\ell\to\ell$. A \emph{framing} of $\ell$ is a slope $\ell''$
on $\partial\nu\ell$ meeting the meridian $m$ once; the framings form a
$\mathbb Z$-torsor under $\ell''\mapsto\ell''+m$. For a framing $\ell''$, let
\[
 Q(\ell'')=(Q\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu\ell)\cup(S^1\times D^2)
\]
be the Dehn filling in which $\{\mathrm{pt}\}\times\partial D^2$ is glued to
$\ell''$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{std:lem:frame}
The homotopy class of $\lambda(\ell'')$ depends only on $\ell''$, and
$\lambda(\ell'')$ and $\lambda(\ell''+m)$ are the two distinct
normal-framing classes of $\gamma$. Consequently, for every framing $\ell''$,
the two framed surgeries on $\gamma$ are the surgeries with framings
$\lambda(\ell'')$ and $\lambda(\ell''+m)$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Tubular maps with a prescribed framing form a connected family. Two
equivariant trivializations in which $\gamma$ is the constant section differ
by a map $\nu\ell\to S^1$ that is identically one on $\ell$, and such a map is
homotopic to the constant map rel $\ell$. Hence, the homotopy class of
$\lambda(\ell'')$ is well defined. Replacing $\ell''$ by $\ell''+m$ changes the
tubular map by $(a,z)\mapsto(a,e^{2\pi ia}z)$ for $a\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$. This fixes the
$h$-direction and turns the $D^2$-directions once around $\gamma$, so the two
frames differ by the loop $a\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(R_{2\pi a},1)$ in $SO(3)$. That loop
represents the generator of $\pi_1(SO(3))\cong\mathbb Z/2$, and there are exactly
two framing classes (Lemma~\ref{lem:frame}).
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{std:prop:torus}
In the setting of Definition~\ref{std:def:data}, let $\Sigma$ be the result
of surgery on $\gamma$ with framing $\lambda(\ell'')$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $\Sigma$ contains a smoothly embedded two-sphere $S_T$ with trivial
      normal bundle, obtained from $T_\ell$ by surgery along $\gamma$.
\item Surgery on $S_T$ gives
      \[
       Y'(\ell''):=(Y\setminus\operatorname{int} P)\cup_{\partial P}(S^1_m\times V).
      \]
      Here $S^1_m=\partial D^2$, $V$ is the solid torus bounded by
      $S^1_a\times S^1_h$ in which $S^1_a\times\{\mathrm{pt}\}$ bounds a disc,
      and the gluing is the identity on
      $\partial P=S^1_a\times S^1_m\times S^1_h$.
\item The action on $Y\setminus\operatorname{int} P$ extends to a smooth effective circle
      action on $Y'(\ell'')$ without fixed points, free on $S^1_m\times V$.
      Its orbit space is $Q(\ell'')$. Its nonfree orbits, with their isotropy
      groups and slice representations, are those of $Y$.
\item $\Sigma$ is obtained from $Y'(\ell'')$ by a framed surgery on an
      embedded circle $\delta$, the core of the sphere surgery.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Put $Y_0=D^2\times S^1_h$, a solid torus with core
$C_0=\{0\}\times S^1_h$, so that $P=S^1_a\times Y_0$,
$\gamma=S^1_a\times\{y_0\}$ with $y_0=(0,1)$, and $T_\ell=S^1_a\times C_0$.
Let $B\subset Y_0$ be a small round ball about $y_0$. The core $C_0$ crosses
$\partial B$ in two points $n$ and $s$. Surgery with the product framing
replaces $S^1_a\times B$ by $D^2\times\partial B$, so
\[
 \Sigma=(Y\setminus\operatorname{int} P)\cup P',\;\;\;
 P'=\bigl(S^1_a\times(Y_0\setminus\operatorname{int} B)\bigr)\cup_{S^1_a\times\partial B}
    (D^2\times\partial B).
\]

(i) Let $c=C_0\setminus\operatorname{int} B$, an arc from $n$ to $s$, and put
\[
 S_T=(S^1_a\times c)\cup\bigl(D^2\times\{n,s\}\bigr).
\]
This is an annulus capped by two discs, and it is the result of surgering
$T_\ell$ along $\gamma$. Let $N_c$ be a regular neighbourhood of $c$ in
$Y_0\setminus\operatorname{int} B$, meeting $\partial B$ in two polar caps $D_n$ and $D_s$.
After the corners have been rounded,
$\nu S_T=(S^1_a\times N_c)\cup(D^2\times(D_n\cup D_s))$ is a tubular
neighbourhood of $S_T$, and the product structures of the two pieces agree
along their intersection. So the normal bundle is trivial.

(ii) Let $N_0=B\cup N_c$, a solid-torus regular neighbourhood of $C_0$. Its
boundary is the union of the annuli $A=\partial B\setminus\operatorname{int}(D_n\cup D_s)$
and $A'=\partial N_c\setminus\operatorname{int} B$; the core of $A$ is the equator of
$\partial B$, a meridian circle of $C_0$. Since $Y_0\setminus\operatorname{int} N_0$ is a
collar $\partial Y_0\times[0,1]$, we have
\[
 P'\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu S_T
 =\bigl(S^1_a\times(Y_0\setminus\operatorname{int} N_0)\bigr)\cup_{S^1_a\times A}(D^2\times A).
\]
Write $\partial Y_0=S^1_m\times S^1_h$. In the collar coordinates
we have $A=S^1_m\times I$ for an arc $I\subset S^1_h$, and therefore
\[
 P'\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu S_T\ \cong\
 S^1_m\times\Bigl(\bigl(S^1_a\times S^1_h\times[0,1]\bigr)
   \cup_{S^1_a\times I\times\{0\}}(D^2\times I)\Bigr)
 = S^1_m\times\bigl(V\setminus\operatorname{int} B'\bigr),
\]
where $B'$ is a ball. Indeed, attaching the three-dimensional two-handle
$D^2\times I$ along $S^1_a\times I\times\{0\}$ turns
$S^1_a\times S^1_h\times[0,1]$ into a solid torus minus a ball, whose meridian
is $S^1_a\times\{\mathrm{pt}\}$. The remaining boundary component is
$S^1_m\times\partial B'=\partial\nu S_T$, and the circles
$\{x\}\times S^1_m$ are meridians of $S_T$: near the caps they are parallel to
$\partial D_n$, and along the annulus they are meridians of the arc $c$.
Surgery on $S_T$ glues in $B'\times S^1_m$, which gives (ii).

(iii) Write $V=D^2_a\times S^1_h$ with $\partial D^2_a=S^1_a$. Rotation of the
factor $S^1_h$ is a free action on $S^1_m\times V$ that agrees with the given
action on $\partial P$. Its orbit space is the solid torus $S^1_m\times D^2_a$,
attached to $Q\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu\ell$ along
$\partial\nu\ell=S^1_a\times S^1_m$ with meridian $S^1_a\times\{\mathrm{pt}\}$.
By the choice of the tubular map this curve is $\ell''$. Nothing changes
outside $P$.

(iv) Surgery on the circle $\delta=\{0\}\times S^1_m$ in $B'\times S^1_m$,
with the framing given by the product structure, reverses the sphere surgery.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{std:rem:BS}
The composite operation $Y\rightsquigarrow\Sigma\rightsquigarrow Y'(\ell'')$ is
the torus surgery on $T_\ell$ whose new meridian is the
$\lambda(\ell'')$-push-off of $\gamma$. Thus, Proposition~\ref{std:prop:torus}
is an equivariant refinement, in the present local setting, of the standard
round-handle factorization cited immediately before its proof. The circle
action is never used on $\Sigma$ itself. Torus surgery on tori in $S^4$ and
its relation to circle and sphere surgeries are also discussed in
\cite{Larson2018}. Iwase \cite{Iwase1988} showed that a Gluck twist of $S^4$
is a multiplicity-one logarithmic transformation on a stabilization of the
sphere; see \cite[arXiv preprint, Theorem~1.9]{NaylorSchwartz2020}. For circle
actions on $S^4$, the decomposition into a twin neighbourhood and the product of $S^1$ with a
knot exterior, and the effect of a framing change on the gluing, are described
in \cite[Section~3]{FintushelSternSunukjian2009}; earlier standardness
arguments for homotopy four-spheres obtained by regluing twin neighbourhoods
are given in \cite[Section~6]{Plotnick}.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{std:lem:exact}
Let $Y'$ be a closed connected oriented smooth four-manifold with a smooth
effective circle action without fixed points, and write $Q'$ for its orbit
orbifold. Let $h\in\pi_1(Y')$ be the class of a principal orbit. Then $h$ is central,
and the orbit map induces an exact sequence
\[
 \langle h\rangle\to\pi_1(Y')\to\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q')
 \to1.
\]
If $O$ is an exceptional orbit with isotropy of order $k$, then $[O]^k$ is
conjugate to $h^{\pm1}$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Centrality follows from Lemma~\ref{per:lem:gottlieb}. For exactness, use
the Borel model
\[
                 BQ'=ES^1\times_{S^1}Y'
\]
for the classifying space of the orbit orbifold. The diagonal circle
action on $ES^1\times Y'$ is free, so
\[
 S^1\to ES^1\times Y'\to BQ'
\]
is an ordinary principal circle bundle. Since $ES^1$ is contractible,
its homotopy exact sequence gives
\[
 \pi_1(S^1)\to\pi_1(Y')
       \to\pi_1(BQ')\to1.
\]
Here $\pi_1(BQ')=\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q')$, and the image of the fibre homomorphism
is $\langle h\rangle$. This proves the asserted exactness even
when that homomorphism is not injective. The classifying-space
description of Seifert fibrations and orbifold fundamental groups is
given in \cite[Corollary~3.1.5 and Sections~4.2.1, 4.3.3,
pp.~83, 91, 95]{Haefliger1984}; compare also
\cite{LeeRaymond2010,Fintushel1978}. For $M_7$ the sequence is the
central extension \eqref{per:eq:centralext}, and in dimension three
it specializes to the familiar sequence for Seifert fibrations
\cite{Scott1983}.

The last assertion follows from the slice model
$S^1\times_{C_k}D^3$, which deformation retracts onto $O$ and in
which a principal orbit winds $k$ times around $O$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{std:prop:cyclic}
If $\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q')$ is finite cyclic, then $Y'\cong_{\mathrm{diff}} S^3\times S^1$ and
$\Sigma\cong_{\mathrm{diff}} S^4$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{std:lem:exact}, $\pi_1(Y')$ is a central extension of a cyclic
group by the cyclic group $\langle h\rangle$. It is therefore abelian, so
$\pi_1(Y')\cong\mathbb Z$ by \eqref{std:eq:H1}. Let $n=|\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q')|$. Since
$H_1(Y')/\langle h\rangle$ is finite of order $n$, we have $h=\tau^{\pm n}$ for
a generator $\tau$.

Since $h$ has infinite order, the action is injective in Chen's sense.
We verify the irreducibility hypothesis in the cited classification.
Injectivity implies that $Q'$ contains no bad two-suborbifold; hence it
admits a finite manifold cover
\cite[Section~2 and the proof of Theorem~1.4]{Chen2015}.
Since $\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q')$ is finite, the universal orbifold cover of $Q'$ is a
closed simply connected three-manifold and is therefore diffeomorphic to
$S^3$ \cite{PerelmanEntropy,PerelmanSurg,PerelmanExt}. Its finite deck action is smoothly
conjugate to an isometric action by \cite[Theorem~E]{DinkelbachLeeb}.
Consequently $Q'$ is spherical and, in particular, irreducible, so $Y'$ is an
irreducible $S^1$-four-manifold in the terminology of \cite{Chen2015}.
Now $\pi_1(Y')\cong\mathbb Z$ is double-ended, and
\cite[Theorem~1.6(2)]{Chen2015} identifies $Y'$ with the mapping torus of a
periodic diffeomorphism $g$ of an elliptic three-manifold $F$.
The mapping-torus exact sequence embeds the finite group $\pi_1(F)$ in
$\pi_1(Y')\cong\mathbb Z$, so $\pi_1(F)=1$ and $F\cong_{\mathrm{diff}} S^3$.
Orientability of $Y'$ implies that $g$ preserves orientation. By Cerf's
theorem \cite{Cerf1968}, $g$ is isotopic to the identity, and hence
$Y'\cong_{\mathrm{diff}} S^3\times S^1$.

By \eqref{std:eq:H1}, $\delta$ represents a generator of
$\pi_1(Y')\cong\mathbb Z$, as does $\{\mathrm{pt}\}\times S^1$.
Freely homotopic embedded circles in a four-manifold are isotopic
(Lemma~\ref{lem:circle-spin}). Both normal-framing classes yield the
standard four-sphere, as follows. Fix
$x_0\in\partial D^4=S^3$, and choose a loop
$R_t$ in the stabilizer $SO(3)\subset SO(4)$ of $x_0$ such that $R_t$ represents the
nontrivial element of $\pi_1(SO(3))$. Then the map
\[
   F:D^4\times S^1\to D^4\times S^1,
   \;\;\;
   F(x,e^{2\pi i t})=(R_t x,e^{2\pi i t})
\]
is a diffeomorphism that fixes the attaching circle
$\{x_0\}\times S^1$ pointwise and changes its normal framing by the
nontrivial element of $\pi_1(SO(3))$. Hence, the two five-dimensional
two-handle attachments along this circle are diffeomorphic. For the product
framing the two-handle cancels the unique one-handle of
$D^4\times S^1$, leaving a five-ball; consequently the boundary after either
framed circle surgery is $S^4$ \cite{GS,Gluck1962}. Therefore, $\Sigma\cong_{\mathrm{diff}} S^4$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{std:prop:dihedral}
Suppose that $\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q')$ is dihedral of order $2p$ with $p$ odd, and that
$Y'$ has an exceptional orbit $e$ with isotropy of order two. Then
$\Sigma\cong_{\mathrm{diff}} S^4$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Since $p$ is odd, the abelianization of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q')$ is $\mathbb Z/2$. By
Lemma~\ref{std:lem:exact} and \eqref{std:eq:H1}, $h$ has degree $\pm2$, and
$e$ has degree $\pm1$ because $e^2$ is conjugate to $h^{\pm1}$. Let $K$ be the
commutator subgroup of $\pi_1(Y')$. It maps onto the commutator subgroup
$C_p$ of the dihedral group, with kernel $K\cap\langle h\rangle$. This kernel
is trivial because $h^k$ has degree $\pm2k$. Thus, $K\cong C_p$, and
$\pi_1(Y')=K\rtimes\langle t\rangle$ for any element $t$ of degree one. The
image of $t$ in the dihedral group is a reflection, since its image in the
abelianization is nonzero, so $t$ acts on $K$ by inversion. For $y\in K$,
\[
 y\,t\,y^{-1}=y\,(t\,y^{-1}t^{-1})\,t=y^2t,
\]
and squaring is a bijection of $C_p$. Hence, all elements of degree one are
conjugate. Orient $\delta$ and $e$ to have degree one; they are then freely
homotopic, hence isotopic, and the isotopy transports the framing. So
$\Sigma$ is obtained by a framed surgery on the orbit $e$. By
Lemma~\ref{fa:lem:orbit-surgery}, the resulting manifold carries an effective smooth
circle action for either framing class. A smooth homotopy four-sphere
admitting an effective smooth circle action is diffeomorphic to $S^4$
\cite{Pao,FintushelHomotopy,Fintushel1978}; see also
Remark~\ref{fa:rem:Pao}.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{std:def:belt}
Fix one of the two bigons. Let $D\subset S^3$ be a small disc that is transverse to
the plane of the diagram and meets $J$ and $W'$ in one point each between
the two crossings of the bigon. Put $\ell_A=\partial D$
(Figure~\ref{std:fig:belt}). Let $b\subset D$ be the straight arc joining the
two points of $(J\cup W')\cap D$, and let $J\natural_bW'$ be the band sum along
the flat band in the diagram plane that contains $b$. For $s\in\mathbb Z$, let $Q_s$
be the orbifold obtained from $\mathcal O_{W}$ by Dehn surgery on $\ell_A$ with slope
$s\mu_A+\lambda_A$, where $\mu_A$ and $\lambda_A$ are the meridian and the Seifert
longitude of $\ell_A$ in $S^3$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{std:thm:belt}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $\ell_A$ lies in the free part of $\mathcal O_{W}$, is a band sum of a meridian of
      $J$ and a meridian of $W'$, and is admissible in the sense of
      Theorem~\ref{wh:thm:section}.
\item $|Q_0|=S^3$, and the singular circle of $Q_0$ is the knot
      $J\natural_bW'$, which is a trefoil. Hence, $\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q_0)$ is dihedral of
      order six.
\item There exists $s_*\in\{1,-1\}$ with the following property. Put
      $r=3-s_*\in\{2,4\}$. Then $|Q_{s_*}|=S^3_r(J)$ is a lens space, and the
      singular circle of $Q_{s_*}$ is the core of the Heegaard solid torus
      $S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu J$. Consequently $\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q_{s_*})\cong\mathbb Z/2r$, the
      meridian of the singular circle maps to the unique element of order two, and
      the complement of the singular circle is a solid torus.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
(i) The loop $\ell_A$ lies in $S^3\setminus(J\cup W')$, hence in the free part
$|\mathcal O_{W}|\setminus W'$. The disc $D$ meets $J$ and $W'$ once each, so $\ell_A$ is
isotopic, in the complement of $J\cup W'$, to the band sum of a meridian of
$J$ and a meridian of $W'$ along $b$. Such loops are admissible by
Theorem~\ref{wh:thm:section}(ii).

(ii) In $|\mathcal O_{W}|=S^3_{+3}(J)$ the singular circle may be moved by handle slides
over $J$. Let $J^{(3)}$ be a $(+3)$-framed parallel of $J$, pushed slightly off
$\nu J$ and meeting $D$ in one point of the arc $b$, between $J$ and $W'$, and
let $b'\subset b$ be the subarc joining $W'$ to $J^{(3)}$. Slide $W'$ over $J$
along the flat band containing $b'$. The resulting knot
$W''=W'\natural_{b'}J^{(3)}$ is isotopic to $W'$ in $S^3_{+3}(J)$ by an
isotopy supported near this band, the surgery solid torus and the thin annulus
between $\partial\nu J$ and $J^{(3)}$. This support is disjoint from
$\ell_A=\partial D$, so the isotopy fixes $\ell_A$ together with its framings
$s\mu_A+\lambda_A$. Moreover $W''$ is disjoint from $D$: the strands of $W'$
and of $J^{(3)}$ pass through $D$ in opposite directions, and the band sum
along $b'$ removes both intersection points. Now $D$ meets only $J$, once, so
$\ell_A$ is a meridian of $J$ in the complement of $W''$. The slam dunk
\cite[Sections~5.1 and~5.3]{GS} replaces the pair $(J,3)\cup(\ell_A,s)$ by
$(J,3-1/s)$. For $s=0$ the new coefficient is $\infty$: both curves disappear,
$|Q_0|=S^3$, and the singular circle is $W''$. The slam dunk is performed relative to $W''$: its support can be
chosen in a sufficiently thin neighbourhood of $\nu J\cup D$
disjoint from $W''$. The resulting $S^3$ is the unfilled diagram,
with $W''$ unchanged. We now track the band as the chosen surgery-framed
parallel is moved back to $J$.

Make the initial choice of $J^{(3)}$ in a slightly enlarged tubular
neighbourhood $U$ of $J$, disjoint from $W'$. In zero-framed
coordinates $U=S^1\times D^2$, write
\[
 J^{(3)}=\{(\theta,\epsilon v(\theta)):\theta\in S^1\},
 \;\;\; 0<\epsilon<1,\;\;\; \deg v=3.
\]
The map $v:S^1\to S^1$ can be chosen constant on the small attaching
interval $I\subset S^1$ of the band, pointing along the original
flat band there. Arrange the portion of the band in $U$ to run
radially outward from $J^{(3)}$ on $I$, at normal radius at least
$\epsilon$. After the slam dunk, the original neighbourhood $U$
is again present in the unfilled $S^3$, and the annulus
\[
 A=\{(\theta,\rho\epsilon v(\theta)):
                  \theta\in S^1,\ 0\le\rho\le1\}
\]
is disjoint from $W'$ and meets the band only along its edge on
$J^{(3)}$. Move $J^{(3)}$ to
$J_\rho=\{(\theta,\rho\epsilon v(\theta)):\theta\in S^1\}$
while extending the band across the corresponding radial strip
in $A$. The extension is untwisted on $I$, since $v$ is constant
there. After the corners are smoothed, these band sums form an isotopy
of knots for $1\ge\rho\ge0$. At $\rho=0$ the attaching component
is $J$ and the extended band is the original flat band containing
$b$. Thus $W''$ is isotopic to $J\natural_bW'$.

In the diagram, the flat band between the two crossings of the bigon turns
both crossings into nugatory kinks. Explicitly, in the notation of
Figure~\ref{std:fig:belt}, the knot $J\natural_bW'$ runs along one edge of
the band from $J$ to $W'$, then once around $W'$, meeting in order
$c_0$ (over), $c$ (under), $c_3$ (over), $c_2$ (under), $c$ (over) and
$c_1$ (under). It then runs along the other edge of the band back to $J$ and once
around $J$ in the opposite sense, meeting $c_1$ (over), $c_3$ (under),
$c_2$ (over) and $c_0$ (under). The arc of $J$ and the arc of $W'$ that bound
the bigon between $c_0$ and the band form, together with that edge of the
band, a loop through $c_0$ containing no other crossing; the same holds for $c_1$.
Removing these two kinks leaves a three-crossing diagram whose crossings are
met in the cyclic order
\[
   c^{-},\;\; c_3^{+},\;\; c_2^{-},\;\; c^{+},\;\; c_3^{-},\;\; c_2^{+},
\]
where the exponent records an under-passage ($-$) or an over-passage ($+$).
Thus, each crossing is met once over and once under, over- and
under-passages alternate, and the cyclic crossing pattern is
$1\,2\,3\,1\,2\,3$; no
crossing is nugatory, because between the two passages through any crossing
each of the other two crossings occurs exactly once. This is the standard diagram of a trefoil, with the Wirtinger presentation
\cite[Chapter~3]{Rolfsen1976}
\begin{align*}
   \pi_1\bigl(S^3\setminus(J\natural_bW')\bigr)
   &\cong\bigl\langle x_1,x_2,x_3\bigm|
        x_2=x_3^{\,\eta}x_1x_3^{-\eta},\;
        x_3=x_1^{\,\eta}x_2x_1^{-\eta},\;
        x_1=x_2^{\,\eta}x_3x_2^{-\eta}\bigr\rangle\\
   &\cong\langle x,y\mid xyx=yxy\rangle
   \cong\langle a,b\mid a^2=b^3\rangle,
\end{align*}
where $\eta=\pm1$ is the common sign of the three crossings, the second
isomorphism eliminates $x_3$ by means of the second relation (the third
relation then becomes redundant), and the third isomorphism is given by $a=xyx$ and $b=xy$.
This group is nonabelian: imposing $a^2=b^3=1$ gives a surjection onto
$C_2*C_3$ (and, in particular, onto $S_3$). Hence, the knot is not the
unknot. Since it admits the displayed nonnugatory three-crossing diagram, it is a
trefoil (up to mirror image); compare the standard three-crossing diagram in
\cite{Rolfsen1976}. To compute the orbifold group directly,
use the Wirtinger meridians $x$ and $y$ in the middle presentation above. Imposing
the order-two meridian relation gives $x^2=y^2=1$, and with these relations
the braid relation $xyx=yxy$ is equivalent to $(xy)^3=1$. Therefore
\[
 \pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q_0)
  \cong\langle x,y\mid x^2=y^2=(xy)^3=1\rangle
  \cong S_3,
\]
the dihedral group of order six.

(iii) For $s=\pm1$, perform the Rolfsen twist along $D$ with $t=-s$ full twists
\cite[Chapter~9]{Rolfsen1976}, \cite[Section~5.3]{GS}. It changes the
coefficient of $\ell_A$ to the meridional slope $\infty$ (since $1/s+t=0$), so $\ell_A$ disappears. It
changes the coefficient of $J$ to $3+t\,\operatorname{lk}(J,\ell_A)^2=3-s$, and it inserts
$t$ full twists into the two strands through $D$. These two strands already
form one full twist, namely the two crossings of the bigon. For exactly one
sign $s=s_*$ the inserted twist cancels it, and the two crossings disappear by
Reidemeister moves. In the resulting diagram of $J\cup W'_*$ the component $J$ has no
self-crossings and meets $W'_*$ only at the two crossings $c_2$ and $c_3$ of
the other bigon, where $W'_*$ passes under $J$ at $c_2$ and over $J$ at
$c_3$. Let $D_J$ be the spanning disc of $J$ obtained from the flat disc in
the diagram plane by pushing its interior below every arc of $W'_*$, keeping
only a thin collar of $J$ near the plane. The knot $W'_*$ enters this collar
only at $c_2$ and $c_3$, and at $c_3$ it stays above $D_J$. Hence, $D_J$ meets
$W'_*$ in exactly one point, at $c_2$, so that $\operatorname{lk}(J,W'_*)=\pm1$.
Moreover, shrinking $D_J$ onto a small disc
about this point is an isotopy of $J$, in the complement of $W'_*$, onto a
meridian of $W'_*$; thus $J$ is a meridian of $W'_*$ (the linking
number alone would not establish this). Twisting
strands of different components preserves the knot type of each component,
so $W'_*$ is unknotted. Therefore, $J\cup W'_*$ is a Hopf link, and $W'_*$ is the
core of the solid torus $S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu J$.

After $r$-surgery on $J$, the complement of $W'_*$ is the surgery solid torus
$V_J$ together with a collar. Choose its core generator $a$ so that
$\mu_J=a$. Since $r\mu_J+\lambda_J$ bounds a meridian disc of $V_J$, we have
$\lambda_J=a^{-r}$. Put
$\varepsilon=\operatorname{lk}(J,W'_*)\in\{1,-1\}$. In the oriented Hopf-link exterior,
the preferred longitude of $J$ satisfies
$\lambda_J=\mu_{W'_*}^{\,\varepsilon}$, and therefore
$
  \mu_{W'_*}=a^{-\varepsilon r}.
$
Consequently,
$
 \pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q_{s_*})
 =\langle a\mid a^{2r}=1\rangle
 \cong\mathbb Z/2r,
$
and the meridian of the singular circle maps to its unique element of
order two. For the orientations of Figure~\ref{std:fig:belt}, the cancelling
twist gives $\varepsilon=-1$, so the oriented meridian is $a^r$ in the
infinite cyclic group of the singular-circle exterior. In particular, it
is $a^4$ when $s_*=-1$ and $r=4$, in agreement with the peripheral
calculation below.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{std:rem:sstar}
For the mirror image fixed in Section~\ref{wh:sec:whitehead}, we have $s_*=-1$
and $r=4$; thus $|Q_{s_*}|=L(4,1)$ and $\pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q_{s_*})\cong\mathbb Z/8$. Indeed, for
the orientations of Figure~\ref{std:fig:belt} the crossings $c_0$ and $c_1$ are
positive, so the right-hand bigon contributes $+1$ to $\operatorname{lk}(J,W')$, and
$\operatorname{lk}(J,\ell_A)=-\operatorname{lk}(W',\ell_A)=-1$. A Rolfsen twist with $t$ full twists along
$D$ changes $\operatorname{lk}(J,W')$ by $t\,\operatorname{lk}(J,\ell_A)\operatorname{lk}(W',\ell_A)=-t$ (compare
\cite[Section~5.3]{GS}), and the inserted twist cancels the bigon exactly when
it contributes $-1$; hence $t=1$ and $s_*=-t=-1$. Reversing an orientation
multiplies both contributions by the same sign, so the conclusion is
independent of the orientations; for the other mirror image we have $s_*=1$ and
$r=2$. The value of $s_*$ is not used in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{std:thm:main}.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{std:rem:belt-peripheral}
For the oriented diagram of Figure~\ref{std:fig:belt}, choose based
meridians $a$, $b$ and $c$ of $J$, $W'$ and $\ell_A$, respectively.
The Wirtinger presentation, with the other arc meridians eliminated,
can be written using the words
$
 u=b^{-1}ab,\;\; d=c^{-1}ac,\;\;
 w=c^{-1}a^{-1}bac,\;\; v=uwu^{-1}
$
and the three relations
$
 d=vuv^{-1},\;\; b=wvw^{-1},\;\;
 c=b^{-1}aca^{-1}b.
$
With these basings the preferred longitudes are
$
 \lambda_J=bv^{-1}c^{-1},\;\; \lambda_A=a^{-1}b.
$
Thus, if $E_s$ is the exterior of the singular circle in $|Q_s|$,
its group is obtained by adding
$
 a^3bv^{-1}c^{-1}=1,\;\; c^sa^{-1}b=1;
$
the orbifold group has the additional relation $b^2=1$.

For $s=0$, the second filling relation gives $b=a$, whence
$u=a$, $w=d$ and $v=ada^{-1}$. The remaining relations reduce to
$dad=ada$ and $c=a^5d^{-1}a^{-1}$; eliminating $c$ gives
\[
 \pi_1(E_0)\cong\langle a,d\mid dad=ada\rangle,
 \;\;\; \mu_{\mathcal S}=a.
\]
Here $d=(ad)a(ad)^{-1}$, so imposing $a^2=1$ also imposes
$d^2=1$ and yields the dihedral group of order six.

For $s=-1$, the belt relation gives $b=ac$, and hence
$u=d=c^{-1}ac$, $w=b$ and $v=dbd^{-1}$. The relation
$b=wvw^{-1}$ gives $v=b$, equivalently $[d,b]=1$.
Since $[d,b]=c^{-1}[a,c]c$, this is $[a,c]=1$.
The $J$-filling relation then gives $c=a^3$ and $b=a^4$;
all the other relations become redundant. Consequently,
\[
 \pi_1(E_{-1})\cong\mathbb Z\langle a\rangle,
 \;\;\; \mu_{\mathcal S}=a^4,
 \;\;\; \pi_1^{\mathrm{orb}}(Q_{-1})\cong\langle a\mid a^8=1\rangle.
\]
These presentations retain the singular meridian and confirm the
group and slope calculations of Theorem~\ref{std:thm:belt}.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{quat:prop:X3-spin}
For both specified surgery framings, $X^{(3)}_\epsilon$ is spin. More
precisely, on the degree-three cover $M_3$ of the mapping torus, the spin
structure
\begin{equation}\label{quat:eq:extending-spin}
   \widehat s_{3,\epsilon}:=s_3+(1-\eta_\epsilon)a_3,
   \;\;\; \eta_+=0,\;\; \eta_-=1,
\end{equation}
extends across the circle surgery that produces
$X^{(3)}_\epsilon$.

Furthermore,
\begin{equation}\label{quat:eq:X3-homology}
 \pi_1(X^{(3)}_\epsilon)=Q_8,
 \;\;\;
 H_1(X^{(3)}_\epsilon;\mathbb Z)
 \cong H_2(X^{(3)}_\epsilon;\mathbb Z)
 \cong (\mathbb Z/2)^2,
 \;\;\; \operatorname{sign}(X^{(3)}_\epsilon)=0.
\end{equation}
The residual $C_3$-action on $X^{(3)}_\epsilon$ fixes exactly one
spin structure.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{nf:lem:calibration} gives
$
 \operatorname{sp}_{s_3}(\gamma_3,\lambda_{\epsilon,3})
   =(-1)^{3\eta_\epsilon}=(-1)^{\eta_\epsilon}.
$
The class $a_3$ evaluates to one on the circle $\gamma_3$ in the positive
base direction. Hence, \eqref{nf:eq:spin-rules} gives
$
 \operatorname{sp}_{\widehat s_{3,\epsilon}}
       (\gamma_3,\lambda_{\epsilon,3})
 =(-1)^{1-\eta_\epsilon}(-1)^{\eta_\epsilon}=-1.
$
By Lemma~\ref{lem:circle-spin}, this is precisely the sign for which
the spin structure extends across the circle-surgery cap. Thus, the
filled manifold is spin for either $\epsilon$.

The fundamental group and integral homology are given by the case
$m\equiv3\pmod6$ of Theorem~\ref{per:thm:tower}; since
$Q_8^{\rm ab}\cong(\mathbb Z/2)^2$, this gives
\eqref{quat:eq:X3-homology}. In particular the rational second homology
vanishes, so the signature is zero.

Spin structures form a torsor over
$H^1(X^{(3)}_\epsilon;\mathbb F_2)\cong\mathbb F_2^2$. The residual order-three
deck transformation acts on $Q_8^{\rm ab}$ by the automorphism induced
by $\alpha$; it cyclically permutes its three nonzero elements. Thus
there is no nonzero invariant element of $H^1$. An order-three action
on the four-element spin-structure torsor must have an orbit of size
one, and two fixed spin structures would have a nonzero invariant
difference. Hence, the fixed spin structure is unique.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{quat:cor:unmarked-delta}
If $\delta_+\ne\delta_-$, then $X^{(3)}_+$ and $X^{(3)}_-$ are not
homotopy equivalent and in particular are not diffeomorphic. Moreover,
$X^{(3)}_+$ and $X^{(3)}_-$ are stably homeomorphic if and only if
$\delta_+=\delta_-$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
The equivariant intersection pairing is preserved by a homotopy
equivalence up to a group automorphism and an overall sign, so the
first assertion follows from \eqref{quat:eq:teichner-sec}.
Stabilization replaces the group-ring pairing by
$
 \lambda_X\ \perp\ \mathsf H(\mathbb Z Q_8)^{\perp r},
$
where $\mathsf H(\mathbb Z Q_8)$ is the hyperbolic form on $(\mathbb Z Q_8)^2$.
A hyperbolic form is a symmetrization. Conversely, restricting a
symmetrization of this orthogonal sum to $\pi_2X$ gives a
symmetrization of $\lambda_X$. Hence $\mathrm{sec}$ is unchanged by
stabilization, and a stable homeomorphism forces
$\delta_+=\delta_-$, even if it reverses orientation or relabels $Q_8$.

Conversely, suppose that $\delta_+=\delta_-$. Both manifolds are spin
and have signature zero by Proposition~\ref{quat:prop:X3-spin}, and
$H_4(Q_8;\mathbb Z)=0$, so the $\pi_1$-fundamental classes vanish. Teichner's
stable classification of closed spin four-manifolds with a common finite
fundamental group whose $2$-Sylow subgroups have periodic cohomology, by
signature, $\pi_1$-fundamental class and $\mathrm{sec}$
\cite[Introduction, Theorem~(4.4.10), p.~5]{Teichner1992}, therefore gives a
stable homeomorphism; its smooth form
\cite[Corollary~4.4.10(1), p.~62]{Teichner1992} gives a stable
diffeomorphism. Since both manifolds have
Euler characteristic two, the numbers of $S^2\times S^2$ summands on
the two sides must agree. No cancellation of these summands is asserted.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{quat:cor:bordism-bit}
Let $u_\epsilon:X^{(3)}_\epsilon\to BQ_8$ be a classifying map, and choose
any spin structure on $X^{(3)}_\epsilon$, for example the unique one
fixed by the residual $C_3$-action. Then
\[
 \delta_\epsilon=0
 \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
 [X^{(3)}_\epsilon,u_\epsilon]=0
 \;\;\text{in}\;\;
 \widetilde\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(BQ_8)\cong\mathbb Z/2.
\]
Thus, computing $\delta_\epsilon$ reduces to a single spin-bordism
computation over $BQ_8$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{quat:prop:X3-spin} the manifold is spin and has
signature zero, so its class lies in the reduced group, which by
\eqref{quat:eq:spin-bordism-Q8} is detected by $\mathrm{sec}$. The class is independent of the chosen spin structure. Indeed,
changing it by
$\beta\in H^1(X^{(3)}_\epsilon;\mathbb Z/2)$ changes the secondary
coordinate by the class of
\[
 u_{\epsilon*}\bigl(\beta\cap[X^{(3)}_\epsilon]_{\mathbb F_2}\bigr)
 \;\;\text{in}\;\;
 H_3(Q_8;\mathbb F_2)/
 \operatorname{im}\bigl(d_2:E^2_{5,0}\to E^2_{3,1}\bigr),
\]
by \cite[Proposition~3.2.4, p.~41]{Teichner1992}.
For $Q_8$ this incoming differential is zero, and
$E^\infty_{3,1}=H_3(Q_8;\mathbb F_2)$ by
Lemma~\ref{eval:lem:e31}. Thus the quotient is canonically identified with the group
$H_3(Q_8;\mathbb F_2)$ used to evaluate the secondary coordinate here. Since $u_\epsilon$ induces an
isomorphism on fundamental groups, $\beta=u_\epsilon^*b$ for some
$b\in H^1(Q_8;\mathbb F_2)$. Moreover, naturality of coefficient reduction gives
\[
 u_{\epsilon*}[X^{(3)}_\epsilon]_{\mathbb F_2}
 =\rho_2\bigl(u_{\epsilon*}[X^{(3)}_\epsilon]_{\mathbb Z}\bigr)=0,
\]
because $H_4(BQ_8;\mathbb Z)=0$. The projection formula therefore makes the
cap-product expression zero. The signature and the secondary coordinate are
unchanged, so \eqref{quat:eq:spin-bordism-Q8} gives the same bordism class.
An elementary proof of this independence, using point preimages, is given in
Remark~\ref{eval:rem:spin-independence}.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{quat:prop:M3-bordism}
For each $\epsilon$, the five-dimensional trace of the circle surgery
$(M_3,\gamma_3,\lambda_{\epsilon,3})$ is a spin bordism over $BQ_8$
from
$
 (M_3,\widehat s_{3,\epsilon},\bar u)
$
to $(X^{(3)}_\epsilon,s^{\rm out}_\epsilon,u_\epsilon)$, where
$\widehat s_{3,\epsilon}$ is defined in \eqref{quat:eq:extending-spin}, and
$s^{\rm out}_\epsilon$ and $u_\epsilon$ are obtained by restricting the
extended spin structure and map, respectively, to the outgoing end of the
trace. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{quat:eq:M3-bordism-equality}
 [X^{(3)}_\epsilon,u_\epsilon]
   =[M_3,\widehat s_{3,\epsilon},\bar u]
 \;\;\text{in }\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(BQ_8),
\end{equation}
and $\delta_\epsilon$ is the $\mathbb Z/2$-coordinate of the right-hand side.
In particular,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
   \delta_+&=\mathrm{sec}_{BQ_8}
      [M_3,s_3+a_3,\bar u],\\
   \delta_-&=\mathrm{sec}_{BQ_8}
      [M_3,s_3,\bar u].
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here $\mathrm{sec}_{BQ_8}$ is the secondary $\mathbb Z/2$-coordinate of the
bordism class over $BQ_8$ in \eqref{quat:eq:spin-bordism-Q8}.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
The surgery trace is obtained from $M_3\times I$ by attaching a
five-dimensional two-handle along the framed circle. By
Proposition~\ref{quat:prop:X3-spin}, the source spin structure
$\widehat s_{3,\epsilon}$ restricts to the bounding spin structure on that
attaching circle, so it extends across the handle. The homomorphism
\eqref{quat:eq:M3-to-Q8} sends $[\gamma_3]=t_3$ to the identity, and
therefore the map $\bar u$ extends across the same handle. On the
outgoing boundary, the surviving fundamental group is $Q_8$ and the
extended map induces the identity on this group, so it is a classifying
map. This proves \eqref{quat:eq:M3-bordism-equality}; the final two formulas
follow from Corollary~\ref{quat:cor:bordism-bit} and
\eqref{quat:eq:extending-spin}.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{eval:lem:e31}
Consider the Atiyah--Hirzebruch spectral sequence
$E^2_{p,q}=H_p(BQ_8;\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_q)\Rightarrow
\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_{p+q}(BQ_8)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $E^2_{4,0}=H_4(Q_8;\mathbb Z)=0$, $E^2_{1,3}=0$, and
      $E^2_{3,1}=H_3(Q_8;\mathbb Z/2)\cong\mathbb Z/2$.
\item $E^\infty_{3,1}=E^2_{3,1}$ and $E^\infty_{2,2}=0$. Hence, the
      reduced group $\widetilde\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(BQ_8)$, which is the
      torsion subgroup of $\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(BQ_8)$, maps isomorphically
      onto $E^\infty_{3,1}\cong\mathbb Z/2$.
\item $\iota_*:H_3(\mathcal Q;\mathbb Z/2)\to H_3(Q_8;\mathbb Z/2)$ is an
      isomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
The free action of $Q_8$ on $S^3$ gives a periodic resolution, so
$H_p(Q_8;\mathbb Z)$ is $\mathbb Z$, $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$, $0$, $\mathbb Z/8$ and $0$ for $p=0,\dots,4$, respectively; compare
\cite[Lemma~4.1.1(b)]{Teichner1992}. Together
with $\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_3=0$ and the universal coefficient theorem, this
gives~(i).

In Teichner's spectral-sequence framework the secondary invariant in
\eqref{quat:eq:spin-bordism-Q8} is the component of a bordism class in
$E^\infty_{3,1}$ \cite{Teichner1992}. The isomorphism
\eqref{quat:eq:spin-bordism-Q8} therefore gives
$E^\infty_{3,1}\cong\mathbb Z/2=E^2_{3,1}$. Since $E^\infty_{4,0}$ and
$E^\infty_{1,3}$ vanish by~(i), the only remaining filtration quotient of
the reduced group, $E^\infty_{2,2}$, is zero. The reduced group is the
torsion subgroup because $\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4\cong\mathbb Z$ is detected by the
signature.

The same equality follows from the spectral-sequence differentials.
Differentials leaving $E^r_{3,1}$ land in $E^2_{1,2}$ or in
$E^3_{0,3}=0$. The differential with the first target is dual to $\operatorname{Sq}^2$ on
$H^1(Q_8;\mathbb F_2)$; this operation vanishes for degree reasons. The only differential
entering $E^r_{3,1}$ is $d_2:E^2_{5,0}\to E^2_{3,1}$, which is reduction modulo two
followed by the dual of
$\operatorname{Sq}^2:H^3(Q_8;\mathbb F_2)\to H^5(Q_8;\mathbb F_2)$; this is the
standard description of the first differentials
\cite[Lemma~2.3.2 and Theorem~3.1.3]{Teichner1992}, \cite{Teichner1993}. In the classical presentation
\[
 H^*(Q_8;\mathbb F_2)=\mathbb F_2[x,y,e]/(x^2+xy+y^2,\ x^2y+xy^2),
 \;\;\; |x|=|y|=1,\;\; |e|=4
\]
\cite{AdemMilgram} (equivalently
$\mathbb F_2[x,y,e]/(x^2+xy+y^2,\ x^3)$, the form used in
\cite[Lemma~4.1.1(b)]{Teichner1992}, since $x^3=x^2y+xy^2$ modulo the
first relation), the group $H^3$ is spanned by $x^2y$, and
$x^3=x(xy+y^2)=0$. The Cartan formula gives
$\operatorname{Sq}^2(x^2y)=x^4y=0$.
All products of degree-one classes vanish in degrees at least four
\cite[remark following Lemma~4.1.1, p.~50]{Teichner1992}.
The required Steenrod-square vanishings follow directly from
instability and the Cartan formula, as in the calculation above.

Finally, $\iota$ is $3$-connected, so $\iota_*$ is onto in degree three
for every coefficient group. Both groups in~(iii) have order two.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{eval:rem:e22}
The vanishing of $E^\infty_{2,2}$ in Lemma~\ref{eval:lem:e31}(ii) requires
the $d_3$ differential. Indeed,
$E^2_{2,2}=H_2(Q_8;\mathbb F_2)\cong\mathbb F_2^{\,2}$. The differential
$d_2:E^2_{4,1}\to E^2_{2,2}$ is dual to
$\operatorname{Sq}^2:H^2(Q_8;\mathbb F_2)\to H^4(Q_8;\mathbb F_2)$, which vanishes because
$\operatorname{Sq}^2(xy)=x^2y^2=0$ and $\operatorname{Sq}^2(y^2)=y^4=0$ in the
presentation used in the proof (where $y^3=0$). The differential leaving
$E^2_{2,2}$ has target $E^2_{0,3}=0$. Hence, $E^3_{2,2}\cong\mathbb F_2^{\,2}$, and
$E^\infty_{2,2}=0$ is equivalent to
\[
   d_3:E^3_{5,0}=H_5(Q_8;\mathbb Z)\cong(\mathbb Z/2)^2\to E^3_{2,2}
\]
being an isomorphism. This is precisely Teichner's
Proposition~4.2.1 \cite[Proposition~4.2.1, p.~51]{Teichner1992}. The value
$\widetilde\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(BQ_8)\cong\mathbb Z/2$ is also listed in
\cite[Appendix~A, Table~6]{DavighiGripaiosLohitsiri}.
The same value, and the vanishing of $E^\infty_{2,2}$ through this $d_3$,
are also derived in \cite[Appendices~A.3 and~B]{DavighiGripaiosLohitsiri}
from the computation of the connective real $K$-theory of $BQ_8$ by Bayen and
Bruner \cite{BayenBruner1996}, using the isomorphism
$\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_n(X)\cong ko_n(X)$ for $n\le7$. Together with the survival of $E_{3,1}$, this gives the stated value of
the bordism group and forces the displayed $d_3$ to be an isomorphism.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{eval:lem:compress}
Let $W$ be a closed connected smooth oriented four-manifold and let
$u:W\to BQ_8$ be a map. Then $u$ is homotopic to $\iota\circ g$ for a
smooth map $g:W\to\mathcal Q$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Replace the classifying map
$\iota:\mathcal Q=S^3/Q_8\to BQ_8$ by a fibration in its homotopy class.
Its homotopy fibre is homotopy equivalent to the universal cover $S^3$.
Thus, the fibre is $2$-connected, and for the four-dimensional CW complex $W$
the only possible obstruction to lifting $u:W\to BQ_8$ through $\iota$ lies,
by obstruction theory for sections of fibrations with local coefficients
\cite[Chapter~VI]{WhiteheadGW}, in
\[
     H^4\bigl(W;\pi_3(S^3)\bigr)=H^4(W;\mathbb Z).
\]
The $Q_8$-action on $\pi_3(S^3)\cong\mathbb Z$ is trivial because the deck
transformations preserve orientation. The universal obstruction is therefore
a class $\kappa\in H^4(BQ_8;\mathbb Z)$. Teichner's integral homology calculation
\cite[Lemma~4.1.1(b)]{Teichner1992}, together with the universal coefficient
theorem, gives
\[
                 H^4(BQ_8;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/8.
\]
Hence, $\kappa$ is torsion. Since $W$ is closed, connected and oriented,
the group $H^4(W;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is torsion-free, so $u^*\kappa=0$. There are no higher
obstructions because $\dim W=4$. Therefore, $u$ is homotopic to
$\iota\circ g$ for a continuous map $g:W\to\mathcal Q$. By smooth
approximation, we may choose $g$ to be smooth.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{eval:def:point}
Let $(W,s)$ be a closed spin four-manifold, let $g:W\to\mathcal Q$ be a smooth
map, and let $p\in\mathcal Q$ be a regular value. Frame the normal bundle of the
closed one-manifold $g^{-1}(p)$ by pulling back a positive frame of
$T_p\mathcal Q$, and use this framing to induce a spin structure on this
one-manifold from $s$. The \emph{point-preimage bit}
$\mathfrak p(W,s,g)\in\mathbb Z/2$ is the class of this framed spin
one-manifold in $\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_1\cong\mathbb Z/2$, that is, the number of its
components with closing sign $+1$, modulo two. When the spin structure
and the map are clear, we write $\mathfrak p(W)$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{eval:lem:point}
In Definition~\ref{eval:def:point}, the image of $[W,s,\iota\circ g]$ in
$\widetilde\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(BQ_8)\cong\mathbb Z/2$ is $\mathfrak p(W,s,g)$.
Consequently $\mathfrak p(W,s,g)$ depends only on $(W,s)$ and on the
homotopy class of $\iota\circ g$. If $W$ has signature zero, then
$[W,s,\iota\circ g]=0$ in $\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(BQ_8)$ if and only if
$\mathfrak p(W,s,g)=0$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Use a CW structure on $\mathcal Q$ with a single three-cell containing
$p$. Since $\dim\mathcal Q=3$, the Atiyah--Hirzebruch filtration satisfies
$F_3\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(\mathcal Q)=\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(\mathcal Q)$. Its top
quotient is
$
   F_3/F_2=E^\infty_{3,1}(\mathcal Q).
$
No differential affects $E_{3,1}(\mathcal Q)$: the possible $d_2$ source
$E^2_{5,0}$ is zero for dimensional reasons, while the possible $d_2$ differential with target
$E^2_{1,2}$ is dual to
$\operatorname{Sq}^2:H^1(\mathcal Q;\mathbb Z/2)\to H^3(\mathcal Q;\mathbb Z/2)$,
which is zero; the possible $d_3$ target has coefficient
$\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_3=0$, and there are no higher possibilities. Hence
$
   E^\infty_{3,1}(\mathcal Q)=H_3(\mathcal Q;\mathbb Z/2)\cong\mathbb Z/2.
$
More explicitly, the quotient by the two-skeleton gives the natural
relative-bordism map
\[
 \Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(\mathcal Q)
 \to
 \Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(\mathcal Q,\mathcal Q^{(2)})
 \cong
 \widetilde\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(S^3)
 \cong
 \Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_1.
\]
The relative group is the coefficient group on the unique top cell.
The kernel of this map is $F_2$ by the exact sequence of the pair,
and the preceding differential calculation shows that the induced
map on $F_3/F_2$ is an isomorphism onto $\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_1\cong\mathbb Z/2$.
The geometric description of the Atiyah--Hirzebruch spectral sequence
identifies the coefficient on a cell with the bordism class of a
regular-value preimage, equipped with its induced structure
\cite[Theorem~1.1 and the preceding paragraph, p.~172]{Tene2017}.
In the form used here, the edge map
$\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_n(Y^{(k)})\to H_k(Y^{(k)};\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_{n-k})$ of a
$k$-dimensional CW complex $Y^{(k)}$ sends the class of a map to
$\sum_i[N_i]\,e^k_i$, where $N_i$ is the framed, hence spin, regular preimage
of the barycentre of the $k$-cell $e^k_i$ \cite[Lemma~2.5]{KPT2020}.
Here the suspension identification frames the normal directions by
a positive frame of $T_p\mathcal Q$, so the induced spin structure
is exactly the one in Definition~\ref{eval:def:point}.
Consequently this map sends $[W,s,g]$ to $\mathfrak p(W,s,g)$.
Changing the positive frame through positive frames gives a
framing homotopy, and transversality applied to a homotopy of maps
gives the corresponding spin bordism of regular preimages
\cite[Chapter~3]{Hirsch}.

The map $\iota$ induces a morphism of spectral sequences, which on
$E^\infty_{3,1}$ is the isomorphism supplied by
Lemma~\ref{eval:lem:e31}(ii) and~(iii).
The class $\iota_*[W,s,g]$ and its reduced part differ by the image of
$[W,s]\in\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4$, which has filtration zero. Hence, the reduced
part has image $\mathfrak p(W,s,g)$ in $E^\infty_{3,1}(BQ_8)$, and
Lemma~\ref{eval:lem:e31}(ii) identifies the reduced group with this
quotient. The final assertion holds because a signature-zero class is
torsion.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{eval:rem:spin-independence}
The independence of the spin structure in the proof of
Corollary~\ref{quat:cor:bordism-bit} can also be seen directly from
Definition~\ref{eval:def:point}, without
\cite[Proposition~3.2.4]{Teichner1992}. Let $(W,s)$ be a closed spin
four-manifold, let $g\colon W\to\mathcal Q$ be a smooth map with regular
value $p$, and let $\omega\in H^3(\mathcal Q;\mathbb F_2)$ be the generator. The
mod-two class of the one-manifold $g^{-1}(p)$ is Poincar\'e dual to
$g^*\omega$. If $\beta=g^*b$ with $b\in H^1(\mathcal Q;\mathbb F_2)$, then, by
\eqref{nf:eq:spin-rules}, replacing $s$ by $s+\beta$ multiplies the closing
sign of each component $C$ of $g^{-1}(p)$ by
$(-1)^{\langle\beta,[C]\rangle}$, while the framing is unchanged. Hence
\[
 \mathfrak p(W,s+\beta,g)-\mathfrak p(W,s,g)
 =\bigl\langle\beta,[g^{-1}(p)]\bigr\rangle
 =\bigl\langle g^*(b\cup\omega),[W]_{\mathbb F_2}\bigr\rangle=0,
\]
because $H^4(\mathcal Q;\mathbb F_2)=0$. If $u\colon W\to BQ_8$ induces an
isomorphism on fundamental groups and $u\simeq\iota\circ g$
(Lemma~\ref{eval:lem:compress}), then every $\beta\in H^1(W;\mathbb F_2)$ has this
form, since $\beta=u^*b'=g^*(\iota^*b')$ for some
$b'\in H^1(BQ_8;\mathbb F_2)$. This applies to $X^{(3)}_\epsilon$ and, more
generally, to $X_{\epsilon,3m}$ with $m$ odd, whose fundamental group is
again $Q_8$.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{eval:lem:product}
Every spin structure on $\mathcal Q\times S^1$ is a product
$s_{\mathcal Q}\times\sigma$. For the projection
$\mathrm{pr}:\mathcal Q\times S^1\to\mathcal Q$,
\[
 \mathfrak p(\mathcal Q\times S^1,s_{\mathcal Q}\times\sigma,\mathrm{pr})
 =\begin{cases}1,&\sigma\ \text{is the Lie structure},\\
               0,&\sigma\ \text{bounds}.\end{cases}
\]
Equivalently, the bit is $1$ exactly when a circle $\{x\}\times S^1$ with
a constant normal framing has closing sign $+1$. In particular
$[S^1_{\mathrm{Lie}}]\times[\mathcal Q,s_{\mathcal Q},\iota]$ is the
nonzero element of $\widetilde\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(BQ_8)$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Spin structures on $\mathcal Q\times S^1$ form a torsor over
$H^1(\mathcal Q;\mathbb Z/2)\oplus H^1(S^1;\mathbb Z/2)$, and the eight product
structures are distinct. The preimage of $p$ under $\mathrm{pr}$ is
$\{p\}\times S^1$ with a constant framing. The final assertion follows from
Lemma~\ref{eval:lem:point}.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{eval:prop:transfer}
Let $(W,s)$ be a closed connected spin four-manifold, let $g:W\to\mathcal Q$
be a smooth map, and let $\psi:\pi_1(W)\to D_{14}$ be an epimorphism. Let
$W^{\mathrm{irr}}\to W$ and $W^{\mathrm{reg}}\to W$ be the connected
coverings corresponding to $\psi^{-1}\langle\rho\rangle$ and $\ker\psi$,
of degrees $7$ and $14$, respectively, with the pulled-back spin structures and maps to
$\mathcal Q$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eval:eq:transfer}
 \mathfrak p(W)=\mathfrak p(W^{\mathrm{irr}})+\mathfrak p(W^{\mathrm{reg}})
 \in\mathbb Z/2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Fix a regular value $p$. Its preimage under the map from each covering space
is the lift of $g^{-1}(p)$, with the pulled-back framing and spin structure. Let $C$ be a
component of $g^{-1}(p)$, write $[C]\in\mathbb Z/2$ for its class, and let
$h\in D_{14}$ be the image of its homotopy class, defined up to
conjugacy. The components of its preimage in $W^{\mathrm{irr}}$ and
$W^{\mathrm{reg}}$ correspond, respectively, to the orbits of
$\langle h\rangle$ on $D_{14}/\langle\rho\rangle$ and on $D_{14}$. A
component over an orbit of length $d$ covers $C$ with
degree $d$. Its closing sign is the $d$th power of that of $C$, as in the
proof of Lemma~\ref{nf:lem:calibration}. Thus, a lift of odd degree has
class $[C]$, and a lift of even degree is a Lie circle.

If $h=1$, the two contributions are $7[C]$ and $14[C]$. If $h$ is a
reflection, it fixes exactly one coset of $\langle\rho\rangle$ and
permutes the other six in three transpositions, while it acts on
$D_{14}$ by seven transpositions; the contributions are $[C]+3$ and $7$.
If $h$ is a nontrivial rotation, it has one orbit of length seven on the
cosets and two such orbits on $D_{14}$; the contributions are $[C]$ and
$2[C]$. In each case the two contributions add up to $[C]$ modulo two.
Summing over the components of $g^{-1}(p)$ proves \eqref{eval:eq:transfer}.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{eval:lem:trivialize}
Put $\jmath(s)=\exp(\tfrac{\pi}{2}js)\in S^3$ and
$\widetilde\Upsilon(v,s)=(v\,\jmath(s),s)$ on $S^3\times\mathbb R$. Then
$\widetilde\Upsilon$ commutes with $\gamma_{q,0}$ for every $q\in Q_8$, and
$
 \widetilde\Upsilon(v,s+1)=D_3\,\widetilde\Upsilon(v,s).
$
Hence, $\widetilde\Upsilon$ induces diffeomorphisms
\[
 \Upsilon_1:\mathcal Q\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to M_3^{\mathrm{irr}},
 \;\;\;
 \Upsilon_2:\mathcal Q\times\mathbb R/2\mathbb Z\to M_3^{\mathrm{reg}}.
\]
The circle factors in these two products represent $t_3$ and $t_3^2$, respectively,
and the induced map on $\pi_1(\mathcal Q)=Q_8$ is the identity. For each of the two covers,
the pullback of the map $\bar u$ of \eqref{quat:eq:M3-to-Q8}, composed with
the corresponding $\Upsilon_k$, is homotopic to $\iota\circ\mathrm{pr}$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Right multiplication commutes with the left action of $Q_8$, and
$\jmath(s+1)=\jmath(s)j$ gives the displayed identity by
\eqref{eval:eq:D3}. The path $s\mapsto\widetilde\Upsilon(v_0,s)$
($0\le s\le k$) runs from $(v_0,0)$ to $D_3^k(v_0,0)$, so its projection represents
$t_3^k$. Since $\chi(q)=q$ and $\chi(t_3)=1$ in \eqref{quat:eq:M3-to-Q8},
the induced homomorphism $Q_8\times\mathbb Z\to Q_8$ is the projection. As
$BQ_8$ is aspherical, this determines the map up to homotopy.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{eval:lem:signs}
Let $C_1\subset M_3^{\mathrm{irr}}$ and $C_2\subset M_3^{\mathrm{reg}}$ be
the images under $\Upsilon_1$ and $\Upsilon_2$ of
$\{x_0\}\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ and $\{x_0\}\times\mathbb R/2\mathbb Z$, respectively, each framed by the
image of a constant normal frame. For the pulled-back spin structure $s_3$,
\[
 \operatorname{sp}_{s_3}(C_1)=\operatorname{sp}_{s_3}(C_2)=+1.
\]
Consequently, for the spin structures \eqref{quat:eq:extending-spin},
\begin{equation}\label{eval:eq:product-signs}
 \operatorname{sp}_{\widehat s_{3,\epsilon}}(C_1)=(-1)^{1-\eta_\epsilon},\;\;\;
 \operatorname{sp}_{\widehat s_{3,\epsilon}}(C_2)=+1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Work in the trivialization \eqref{nf:eq:trivialization}. At $(v_0,s)$, the
constant frame whose first vector is the base direction is
$x\mapsto v_0x$, with spin lift $(v_0,1)$. The differential of
$\widetilde\Upsilon$ is right multiplication by $\jmath(s)$ together with
a triangular shear coming from the $s$-derivative of $v_0\jmath(s)$; the
shear can be removed through invertible orientation-preserving fibrewise
maps and does not affect sign comparisons.
To see that the shear is removed through closed loops of frames, write
$x=w+a\,v_0$ with $w\in T_{v_0}S^3$ and $a=\langle x,v_0\rangle\in\mathbb R$. In
\eqref{nf:eq:trivialization} the differential of $\widetilde\Upsilon$ at
$(v_0,s)$ is $x\mapsto x\,\jmath(s)+a\,v_0\jmath'(s)$, where
$\jmath'(s)=\jmath(s)\,\tfrac{\pi}{2}j=\tfrac{\pi}{2}j\,\jmath(s)$. Hence,
for $0\le\tau\le1$, the maps
\[
 x\longmapsto\bigl(x+\tau a\,v_0\tfrac{\pi}{2}j\bigr)\,\jmath(s)
\]
join this differential, at $\tau=1$, to right multiplication by
$\jmath(s)$, at $\tau=0$. Each of them is invertible and orientation
preserving: since $v_0\tfrac{\pi}{2}j$ is orthogonal to $v_0$, the linear map
$x\mapsto x+\tau a\,v_0\tfrac{\pi}{2}j$ is unipotent. This linear map does
not depend on $s$, one has $\jmath(s+1)=\jmath(s)j$, and the derivative of
$D_3$ is right multiplication by $j$ in \eqref{nf:eq:trivialization}.
Together with $\widetilde\Upsilon(v,s+1)=D_3\widetilde\Upsilon(v,s)$, this
shows that every stage of the homotopy is compatible with the deck
identification. Thus it is a homotopy of closed loops of oriented frames in
$M_3^{\mathrm{irr}}$ and in $M_3^{\mathrm{reg}}$, and the closing signs may
be computed at $\tau=0$.
The transported frame $x\mapsto v_0x\,\jmath(s)$ therefore
has the lift
\[
 G(s)=\bigl(v_0,\jmath(s)^{-1}\bigr),\;\;\;
 G(1)=(v_0,-j),\;\;\; G(2)=(v_0,-1).
\]
The lifted path representing $C_1$ ends at the $D_3$-translate of its initial point, and the
prescribed lift of $D_3$ in \eqref{nf:eq:deck-spin} is
$d_3=(\omega^3,j^3)=(1,-j)$. Since $d_3G(0)=(v_0,-j)=G(1)$, the lift
closes. For $C_2$, the deck element is $D_3^2$, with lift $d_3^2=(1,-1)$,
and again $d_3^2G(0)=G(2)$. This proves the first assertion. The second
follows from $\widehat s_{3,\epsilon}=s_3+(1-\eta_\epsilon)a_3$,
$\langle a_3,[C_k]\rangle=k$, and \eqref{nf:eq:spin-rules}.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{eval:thm:bit}
Let $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{sec}}$ denote the nonzero element of
$\widetilde\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_4(BQ_8)\cong\mathbb Z/2$. For each specified framing,
\begin{equation}\label{eval:eq:bit}
 [X_{\epsilon,3},s^{\rm out}_\epsilon,u_\epsilon]
